1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the product rule and the sum rule is/are true?
o: The product rule applies when every stage is needed to build one outcome.
The sum rule applies when exactly one of several mutually exclusive cases is chosen.
The word "or" in English always means that the counts should be added.
Three-letter codes from five letters with no repeats number `5³`.
1.e: Multiply for required stages, add for exclusive cases, and count how choices shrink when repeats are banned.
w: True: Each outcome is a combination of one choice per stage, so the stage counts multiply.
True: The cases never overlap, so the totals simply add.
False: Addition also needs mutually exclusive cases. Overlapping cases need subtraction of the overlap, and a stage that offers a choice still multiplies with other stages.
False: The value `5³` allows repeats such as AAA. With no repeats the choices shrink: `5 × 4 × 3 = 60`.
True: Each of the `n` positions independently has two choices, and every position is needed.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about permutations and combinations is/are true?
o: `P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!` counts ordered selections of `r` objects from `n`.
`C(n, r) = P(n, r)/r!` because each unordered group appears `r!` times among the ordered selections.
If swapping two chosen items gives a different valid outcome, a combination is needed.
1.e: Order matters for permutations; combinations divide out the `r!` internal orders.
w: True: The `r` positions leave `n, n−1, …, n−r+1` choices, whose product is `n!/(n−r)!`.
True: Dividing by `r!` removes the repeated internal orderings of the same group.
False: A different outcome after a swap means order matters, which is the signal for a permutation.
True: The formula `n!/(r!(n−r)!)` is unchanged when `r` and `n−r` are exchanged.
False: `P(n, n) = n!/0! = n!`, the number of full arrangements of `n` objects.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the block method and the gap method is/are true?
o: Six distinct objects in a row with two required adjacent give `5! × 2!` arrangements.
Omitting the internal arrangements of the block undercounts.
If more than `m + 1` special objects must be pairwise non-adjacent among `m` ordinary objects, the count is positive but small.
After choosing the gaps, the order of distinct special objects does not matter.
1.e: Blocks multiply by internal orders; gaps number `m + 1` and need `k!` for distinct special objects.
w: True: The pair becomes one block among five outside objects, and the block has two internal orders.
True: Leaving out the factor `k!` treats the block as having one fixed internal order.
True: There is one gap before the first object, one between each neighbouring pair and one after the last.
False: There are only `m + 1` gaps, so the placement is impossible and the count is 0.
False: Distinct special objects can fill the chosen gaps in `k!` orders, so the count is multiplied by `k!`.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about circular arrangements, the complement rule and the pigeonhole principle is/are true?
o: `n` distinct people at a round table, with rotations identical, give `(n − 1)!` arrangements.
If reflections are also identical, divide `(n−1)!` by 2 for `n ≥ 3`.
Twelve students are enough to guarantee two with the same birth month.
"At least one digit" is counted as all strings minus the strings with no digit.
To guarantee `m` objects in some one of `k` categories you need `k·m` objects.
1.e: Fix one person for circles, subtract the unwanted set, and use `k(m−1)+1` for pigeonhole.
w: True: Fixing one person removes the rotational duplicates, and the rest are arranged relative to them.
True: Each seating and its mirror image are then the same, so the count halves.
False: Twelve students can each have a different month. The guarantee needs `12 + 1 = 13`.
True: The complement is the all-letter set, which is far easier to count than every case with one or more digits.
False: The bound is `k(m−1) + 1`: `k(m−1)` objects can still avoid reaching `m` in any category.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about inclusion–exclusion is/are true?
o: The integers 1–1000 divisible by 3 or 5 number 467.
`333 + 200 = 533` is correct because every multiple is counted once.
The multiples of both 3 and 5 are exactly the multiples of 15, and there are 66 of them up to 1000.
It is used only when the two cases cannot happen together.
1.e: Subtract the overlap once when cases can happen together.
w: True: Elements in both sets are counted twice by `|A| + |B|`, so one copy is removed.
True: Adding 333 multiples of 3 and 200 multiples of 5, then removing the 66 counted twice, gives `333 + 200 − 66 = 467`.
False: The 66 multiples of 15 appear in both lists, so 533 counts them twice.
True: A number divisible by 3 and 5 is divisible by 15, and `⌊1000/15⌋ = 66`.
False: Mutually exclusive cases have an empty overlap and use the plain sum rule. Inclusion–exclusion is for overlapping cases.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about algorithms and the cases of Big-O analysis is/are true?
o: An algorithm needs inputs, outputs and a finite sequence of precise, effective steps.
Efficiency is measured by the programming language and processor speed.
Worst case is the default because average case needs input frequencies that are usually unknown.
The best case is the most representative case because it is the cheapest.
Amortised time divides the total cost of a sequence of operations across them without assuming randomness.
2.e: Measure operation growth, default to the worst case, and know amortised time is not random.
w: True: These are the three parts of the definition; the written form is irrelevant.
False: Those change the constant factor only. Efficiency is how the operation count grows with input size.
True: The worst case is a dependable upper limit, while the average case depends on a stated distribution.
False: The best case is a special, non-representative situation and says little about typical cost.
True: This is the definition used in the notes, in contrast to the average case.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about simplifying Big-O is/are true?
o: `0.0001 · 2.1ⁿ` is bounded by `O(2ⁿ)` because the coefficient is tiny.
For independent inputs, `O(2ᵐ + 2ⁿ)` can always be reduced to `O(2ⁿ)`.
2.e: Drop multipliers, not bases, and keep independent variables.
w: True: A constant multiplier does not change the shape of growth.
True: For large `n` the quadratic term dominates the sum.
False: The base is not a multiplier. `2.1ⁿ / 2ⁿ = 1.05ⁿ` grows without bound, so `2.1ⁿ` eventually overtakes any `c · 2ⁿ`.
True: The larger base dominates the sum.
False: Independent inputs are not comparable: `m` may exceed `n`, so both terms must be kept.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about growth rates is/are true?
o: Doubling `n` makes an `O(n²)` algorithm perform about four times the operations.
Doubling `n` adds about one more operation for an `O(log n)` algorithm.
Doubling `n` doubles the operations of an `O(2ⁿ)` algorithm.
The growth order is `1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!`.
A machine 1000 times faster helps an `n!` algorithm as much as it helps a polynomial one.
2.e: Quadratic quadruples, logarithmic adds one, exponential doubles per extra unit.
w: True: Replacing `n` with `2n` in `n²` gives `(2n)² = 4n²`, four times the work.
True: Since `log₂(2n) = log₂ n + 1`, doubling the input adds a single step.
False: Adding just 1 to `n` doubles the work. Doubling `n` squares it.
True: This is the standard ordering to memorise.
False: It lifts the feasible `n!` size only from about 9.5 to 12.5, while a polynomial algorithm gains a large factor in `n`.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about analysing loops is/are true?
o: `range(0, n, 2)` runs about `n/2` iterations and is `O(n)`.
A loop that doubles its index each pass runs about `log₂ n` iterations.
Consecutive loops over `n` items and `m` items cost `O(nm)`.
Nested independent loops over `n` and `m` items cost `O(nm)`.
A triangular loop whose inner count is `i` costs `Σ i = n(n+1)/2`, which is `O(n²)`.
2.e: Add consecutive blocks, multiply nested loops, sum triangular ones.
w: True: The constant divisor drops out.
True: The index reaches `n` after `log₂ n` doublings.
False: Consecutive blocks add: `O(n + m)`. Multiplication is for nesting.
True: The inner loop runs fully for every outer iteration.
True: Write the summation, then keep the dominant term.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the six-step method and logarithms is/are true?
o: Loop iterations should be counted exactly before simplifying to Big-O.
A function call can be treated as `O(1)` automatically.
The log base does not matter in Big-O.
2.e: Count first, cost calls honestly, and remember log(n²) differs from (log n)².
w: True: Exact counts such as `n/2` or `i` expose constants and summations.
False: A call costs whatever its stated cost is, such as `O(n)`.
True: A change of base introduces only a constant divisor.
True: `log(n²) = 2 log n`, a constant multiple of `log n`.
False: Squaring the logarithm is different from taking the logarithm of a square, and `(log n)²` grows faster than `log n`.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about iterative reasoning and linear search is/are true?
o: An invariant is a fact that stays true before and after every iteration.
A successful linear search takes about `(n + 1)/2` comparisons on average.
An unsuccessful linear search takes only about `n/2` comparisons on average.
Linear search requires the array to be sorted.
When tracing by hand, execute one iteration, record every changed variable and check the stopping condition before the next row.
3.e: Invariants, average cost and the row-by-row trace.
w: True: It is the property that justifies why the loop is correct.
True: The key is equally likely to be at any position from 1 to `n`.
False: An absent key forces every item to be checked, so `n` comparisons.
False: It scans every item and works on any order.
True: Building the table row by row avoids jumping to a final answer.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about binary search is/are true?
o: It requires the array to be sorted.
Its worst case takes about `log₂ n + 1` steps, so it is `O(log n)`.
Searching for 57 in the 15-item sorted example needs 3 comparisons.
The base of the logarithm changes the Big-O class.
w: True: The order is what allows half the region to be discarded.
True: Halving reduces `n` to 1 in `log₂ n` steps, plus one to confirm failure.
False: The first middle check can find the key, so the best case is `O(1)`.
True: The middle indices checked are 7, 3 and 5, and `a[5] = 57`.
False: Changing base only multiplies by a constant, so all bases give `O(log n)`.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about insertion sort is/are true?
o: It keeps the left part of the array sorted.
Its worst case occurs on a strictly reverse-ordered array.
On an already sorted array it takes `O(n²)` time.
It has nested loops because moving the key left is itself a loop.
3.e: Insertion sort is quadratic in the worst case and linear in the best case.
w: True: This is the invariant: `a[0:i]` is sorted before each new key is placed.
True: Every key must slide all the way to the front, giving about `n(n−1)/2` comparisons.
False: Each key is compared once and stays put, so the best case is `O(n)`.
True: The inner loop runs inside the outer loop over positions.
False: Every item must still be examined once, so the best case is `O(n)`, not logarithmic.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about bottom-up merge sort is/are true?
o: The group size doubles at each level, from 1 to 2 to 4 and so on.
Going from size 1 to size `n` takes `log₂ n` levels.
At every level, the merges together touch each element once.
On an already sorted array it runs in `O(n)`.
Small groups move fewer elements per level, so early levels are cheaper.
3.e: Levels times work per level gives `n log n`, in every case.
w: True: Each merge combines two neighbouring sorted groups.
True: Doubling from 1 reaches `n` after `log₂ n` doublings.
True: All pairs together span the whole array, so `n` elements per level.
False: It always performs full merges, so it stays `O(n log n)`.
False: Per level the total is always `n` elements, whatever the group size.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about merging and combining sorting with other steps is/are true?
o: Taking the smaller front value is safe because both inputs are sorted.
Merging lists of lengths `n` and `m` takes `O(n + m)` time.
Insertion sort makes more comparisons than merge sort on an already sorted array.
Binary search can be applied to an unsorted array as long as you start in the middle.
Sorting first and then doing an `O(n)` scan costs `O(n log n)` overall.
3.e: Merging is linear; sort-then-scan is dominated by the sort.
w: True: No smaller value can hide behind either front.
True: Each step advances one index and no index moves backwards.
False: Insertion sort makes about `n` comparisons there, fewer than merge sort's full work.
False: Without order, the discarded half could contain the key.
True: The `O(n log n)` sorting term dominates the added linear term.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the structure of recursive functions is/are true?
o: A recursive function has a contract, a base case, a reduction step and a combination step.
Fibonacci needs only one base case because `fibonacci(n−1)` always reaches it.
A base case written after an unconditional recursive call is dead code, so the recursion never stops.
If the base case is `n == 1` but `n = 0` is possible, subtracting 1 can skip past it.
Recursion depth is the total number of calls made.
4.e: Four parts, enough base cases, and a reachable base case.
w: True: These are the four parts needed for a correct recursive function.
False: It needs two, since `fibonacci(n−2)` can land on either 0 or 1.
True: The recursive call happens before the test is reached on every path.
True: The sequence 0, −1, −2, … never lands on 1.
False: It is the longest chain of simultaneously unfinished calls, which sets memory use.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about tracing `factorial(4)` is/are true?
o: It makes four calls but only three multiplications.
The base case performs a multiplication.
The number of calls always equals the number of operations.
Each unfinished call keeps its own parameters in a stack frame.
4.e: Calls differ from operations, and values return upwards.
w: True: The base call returns 1 without multiplying.
False: It returns the value 1 directly, with no multiplication.
True: Values come up from the base case, one caller at a time.
False: Four calls produce only three multiplications.
True: A paused call must remember its own values until the smaller call returns.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about Fibonacci is/are true?
o: The number of additions grows roughly like `1.6ⁿ`.
A loop that keeps the last two values is `O(2ⁿ)`.
Recursion is automatically more efficient than iteration.
Since `1.6ⁿ < 2ⁿ`, both `O(1.6ⁿ)` and `O(2ⁿ)` are valid upper bounds.
4.e: Repeated subproblems make recursive Fibonacci exponential; the loop is linear.
w: True: The call tree contains repeated subproblems.
True: The ratio of successive counts settles near the golden ratio, about 1.618.
False: The loop runs `n − 1` times, so it is `O(n)`.
False: It is only a different expression of a solution; here it is exponentially slower.
True: Big-O is an upper bound, so the looser bound is still valid.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about halving the exponent when computing a power is/are true?
o: Halving the exponent with two recursive calls per level gives `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) = O(n)`.
Halving the input always gives `O(log n)`.
Saving the half-power and reusing it gives `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n)`.
Reducing the exponent by 1 each time performs about `n` multiplications for exponent `n`.
Writing the same recursive call twice runs it only once because the second result is reused.
4.e: One call per level is what makes halving logarithmic.
w: True: The levels number `log n`, but the call count doubles at each level.
False: It does so only with a single recursive call per level.
True: Only one recursive call remains per level.
True: It is a chain of `n` calls, so `O(n)`.
False: Without saving the result, the call runs twice, completely independently.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about recurrences is/are true?
o: A recursive call may be counted as `O(1)` when computing local work.
4.e: Chains add, geometric sums collapse, and recursive calls are never `O(1)`.
w: True: The constant `c` is added `n` times.
True: There are `log₂ n` calls of constant cost.
False: The sum `n + (n−1) + ⋯ + 1 = n(n+1)/2` is `O(n²)`.
True: The sizes form a geometric sum `n + n/2 + n/4 + ⋯ < 2n`.
False: A recursive call must be written as `T(smaller)`; counting it as `O(1)` hides most of the work.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about stacks and queues is/are true?
o: A stack is last in, first out.
A queue is last in, first out.
A list-based stack with its top at index 0 has `O(n)` push and pop.
A stack with its top at the end of the list has `O(1)` push and pop.
5.e: LIFO against FIFO, and which end of the array matters.
w: True: Only the most recently added item is accessible.
False: A queue is first in, first out: the earliest item is removed first.
True: Every remaining item must shift when the first position changes.
True: `append()` and `pop()` at the end shift nothing.
False: `peek` only inspects the item. `pop` and `dequeue` remove it.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about array-backed queues is/are true?
o: With the head at index 0, `enqueue` is `O(1)`.
With the head at index 0, `dequeue` is `O(1)`.
Whichever end is removable, array operations at that end cost `O(n)`.
A palindrome can be tested by comparing stack pops with queue dequeues of the same characters.
The palindrome test needs only `O(1)` extra space.
5.e: The shifting cost sits at the removable end.
w: True: Appending at the tail shifts nothing.
False: Removing the first item forces every remaining item to shift down, so `O(n)`.
True: The remaining items must shift to close the gap.
True: The stack reverses the order and the queue preserves it.
False: It stores two copies of the input, so `O(n)` extra space.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about priority queues is/are true?
o: `dequeue` returns the best-priority item regardless of arrival order.
A min-heap gives `O(log n)` `enqueue` and `dequeue` and `O(1)` `peek`.
One implementation is best for every access pattern.
5.e: Each implementation moves cost between insertion and removal.
w: True: This differs from a first-in, first-out queue.
True: Insertion appends, but removal must scan for the best item.
False: Finding the position and shifting items costs `O(n)`; its `dequeue` is the cheap one.
True: The heap keeps the best item at the root.
False: The right choice depends on whether enqueue or dequeue is more frequent.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about abstract data types is/are true?
o: An ADT is defined by its operations and hides its representation.
Localisation means a changed implementation does not break client code.
Flexibility means the client must choose the implementation.
A list is a linear structure with one accessible end.
A stack implements the recursive call stack.
5.e: ADTs hide the representation and give localisation and flexibility.
w: True: The client sees what the type does, not how.
True: The client depends only on the operations.
False: It means different implementations can be swapped in without the client noticing.
False: A list allows access at any position, unlike a stack or a queue.
True: Each unfinished call is a frame on a stack, so recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about a queue built from two stacks is/are true?
o: `IN` receives arriving items and `OUT` serves departing items.
Transferring `IN` to `OUT` reverses the order a second time, restoring first-in, first-out.
Each item moves from `IN` to `OUT` at most once, giving amortised `O(1)` per operation.
5.e: Reverse twice and amortise the transfers.
w: True: The two stacks have separate roles.
True: The first reversal is the stack order itself, the second is the transfer.
False: It happens only when `OUT` is empty.
True: The occasional `O(n)` transfer is spread across the operations that follow.
False: A single `dequeue` that triggers a full transfer costs `O(n)`.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about tree terminology is/are true?
o: The root is the topmost node and sits at level 1.
Height is the maximum level of any node, and an empty tree has height 0.
An ancestor is always a direct parent.
A leaf has exactly two children.
6.e: Root at level 1, height is the maximum level.
w: True: Levels start at 1 for the root, with its children at level 2.
True: This is the convention used for levels and heights.
False: An ancestor can be reached through a chain of parent–child links, so it may be indirect.
True: They are children of one node.
False: A leaf has no children at all, so it cannot have two.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about binary tree shapes is/are true?
o: In a full tree every node has 0 or 2 children.
In a complete tree every level except possibly the last is full and the last is packed left.
In a perfect tree all leaves are at the same depth and every internal node has 2 children.
With the root at level 1, a perfect tree of height `h` has `2ʰ − 1` nodes.
6.e: Full, complete, perfect and height-balanced are different properties.
w: True: No node has exactly one child.
True: This describes positions, not child counts.
True: Every level is completely filled.
False: A full tree can have its deepest nodes on the right with gaps on the left, so it need not be complete.
True: The levels hold 1, 2, 4, …, `2ʰ⁻¹` nodes, which sum to `2ʰ − 1`.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about traversals is/are true?
o: Preorder visits the parent before both subtrees.
Inorder of a BST visits keys in ascending order.
Each traversal is `O(n)` because each node is visited once with `O(1)` work.
The postorder of the BST built from 2, 10, 4, 7, 19, 5, 8, 11, 3, 15 starts with 2.
6.e: Parent first, middle or last; all linear.
w: True: The "pre" marks the parent first.
True: The ordering rule puts smaller keys in the left subtree and larger in the right.
False: Postorder visits the parent after both subtrees.
True: The work per visit is constant and every node is visited once.
False: The root 2 is visited last in postorder; that sequence begins with 3.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about binary search trees is/are true?
o: Every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger.
A new key is inserted exactly where a search for it would have failed.
Removing a node with one child lets the parent adopt that child.
Removing a node with two children can use the left-most node of the right subtree.
Removing a leaf requires replacing it with its successor.
6.e: The ordering property drives search, insert and the three removal cases.
w: True: This ordering property defines a BST.
True: The failed search ends at the empty position that keeps the order.
True: The ordering is preserved because the child subtree stays on the same side.
True: This successor is larger than everything on the left and no larger than anything else on the right.
False: A leaf is simply detached by setting the parent's pointer to `None`.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about BST efficiency is/are true?
o: The maximum number of comparisons equals the height of the tree.
A balanced tree of `n` nodes has height about `⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1`, so operations are `O(log n)`.
Inserting already sorted keys one at a time produces a balanced tree.
A completely skewed BST still supports `O(log n)` search.
For a non-empty BST with root at level 1, `⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ ≤ h ≤ n`.
6.e: Cost equals height, and insertion order decides the height.
w: True: Each comparison descends at most one level.
True: Each level roughly doubles the number of nodes.
False: It produces a chain, the worst shape, with `O(n)` operations.
False: Its height is `n`, so search is `O(n)`, no better than a list.
True: The lower bound is the perfect-tree case and the upper bound is the chain.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the definition of a min-heap is/are true?
o: A heap is a complete tree in which every parent is ≤ both children.
The minimum key is at the root.
The inorder traversal of a heap is always sorted.
Searching a heap for an arbitrary key costs `O(n)`.
7.e: Complete shape, parent ≤ children, minimum at the root.
w: True: These are the shape rule and the heap-order rule.
True: No path decreases going down, so the root is smallest.
False: The key 1 is a child of the key 5 at index 1, and 5 > 1 breaks the order rule.
False: A heap orders only parent to child, so inorder is not sorted in general.
True: The heap order does not say which subtree to try.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about storing a heap in a 0-based array is/are true?
o: The left child of index `j` is at `2j + 1`.
The right child of index `j` is at `2j + 2`.
The parent of index `j` is at `⌊(j − 1)/2⌋`.
The last parent is at index `⌊n/2⌋`.
In a 10-entry heap, index 4 has a right child at index 10.
w: True: Levels are stored consecutively, so left children start one past double the index.
True: It sits immediately after the left child.
True: This reverses the child formulas.
False: It is `⌊n/2⌋ − 1` for 0-based indices.
False: Index 10 is not less than 10, so it does not exist.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about heap insertion and removal is/are true?
o: Insertion appends at index `n` because that keeps the tree complete.
Up-heap swaps the new key upward while it is smaller than its parent.
removeMin moves the last entry into the root and then down-heaps.
Down-heap swaps with the larger child.
Insertion and removeMin both cost `O(log n)` because they follow one root-to-leaf path.
w: True: It is the only placement that preserves the shape rule.
True: Each swap fixes one parent–child pair.
True: Removing the last position is the only removal that keeps the tree complete.
False: It swaps with the smaller child; otherwise the new parent would exceed its other child.
True: A path has at most `⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1` nodes.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about BuildHeap is/are true?
o: It runs down-heap from the last parent back to the root.
It is correct bottom-up because both child subtrees are already heaps when a node is repaired.
For a full 15-node tree the maximum swap count is `1·3 + 2·2 + 4·1 + 8·0 = 11`.
The leaves are processed first with down-heap.
w: True: Leaves are already one-node heaps.
True: This is the precondition of down-heap.
False: Most nodes are near the leaves and fall only a short way; the total is `O(n)`.
True: Each node can fall at most as many levels as lie beneath it.
False: Leaves have no children, so they are skipped.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about sorting with a priority queue is/are true?
o: An unsorted-list queue gives selection sort with an `O(n²)` worst case.
A sorted-list queue gives insertion sort with an `O(n²)` worst case.
A heap queue gives heap sort with an `O(n log n)` worst case.
Inserting `n` keys one at a time into a heap costs `O(n)` in total.
In selection sort, phase 1 keeps the queue sorted.
7.e: The queue implementation determines which sort you get.
w: True: Phase 2 scans for the minimum `n` times.
True: Phase 1 inserts each item in place at `O(n)`.
True: Both phases cost `n × O(log n)`.
False: It costs `Σ O(log i) = O(n log n)`; only BuildHeap achieves `O(n)`.
False: Phase 1 only appends; phase 2 scans for the minimum.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about hash functions and collisions is/are true?
o: A good hash function distributes keys uniformly and is deterministic.
A hash function that returns a different random row on each call is acceptable.
The two-stage design turns the key into an integer, then takes the remainder by `N`.
A larger table removes every collision.
With a random hash, 100 words in 1,000 rows have a 99.29% chance of at least one collision.
8.e: Uniform, deterministic, and collisions are frequent.
w: True: Uniformity limits long runs of collisions, and determinism lets a lookup find the same row again.
False: It must be deterministic, or a stored key could never be found again.
True: The remainder keeps the row within `0 … N−1`.
False: Even `N = 100,000` leaves a 4.83% chance of at least one collision among 100 words.
True: Collisions are inevitable and more common than intuition suggests.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about separate chaining is/are true?
o: A large load factor makes lookups generally slower.
Each row holds at most one entry.
Looking up 24 in the example with `N = 7` scans the whole table.
w: True: It is the average bucket length.
True: Buckets can hold any number of entries.
True: Buckets get longer, and a lookup scans one bucket linearly.
False: A row holds a whole bucket list. One entry per row is linear probing.
False: The hash sends 24 to row 3, so only that bucket is scanned.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about linear probing is/are true?
o: A colliding key tries `A[(h(k) + i) % N]` for `i = 1, 2, …` until an empty row is found.
The `% N` makes the probe wrap from the last row back to row 0.
A delete can simply empty the row.
A lookup continues past a deletion marker.
8.e: Wrap-around, markers and a bounded load factor.
w: True: The probe sequence moves forward one row at a time.
True: Without it, the probe could run off the end of the array.
False: An emptied row looks like a never-used row and stops later lookups too early.
True: The marker is not a stopping hole; later keys may lie beyond it.
False: Each row holds at most one entry, so the table can only fill to 1.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the example `N = 7`, `h(k) = k mod 7` inserting 10, 17, 24 and 8 with linear probing is/are true?
o: The key 17 is placed at row 4, after testing rows 3 and 4.
The key 24 is placed at row 5.
The key 8 is placed at row 1.
After deleting 17 and leaving an ordinary empty row 4, a lookup of 24 still finds it.
With a deletion marker at row 4, a lookup of 24 continues to row 5 and finds it.
8.e: Probe sequences, and why markers matter.
w: True: Row 3 is held by 10, so 17 moves to the next free row.
True: Rows 3 and 4 are occupied, so it takes row 5.
True: `8 mod 7 = 1`, and row 1 is empty.
False: The lookup stops at the empty row 4 and reports "not found", although 24 is at row 5.
True: The probe passes the marker and reaches the key.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the cost and use of hash tables is/are true?
o: The worst case for those operations is `O(n)`.
A hash table is the right choice when data must be iterated in sorted order.
A Python `dict` is a hash table and a `set` is a hash table of keys only.
w: True: A uniform hash spreads keys, so the bucket or probe sequence is short.
True: All keys can pile into one bucket or one probe run.
False: `keySet`, `entrySet` and `values` must visit every entry, so `O(n)`.
False: Hashing deliberately scatters keys, so a sorted structure or BST fits better.
True: This is how the two built-in types are implemented.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about graph terminology is/are true?
o: The length of a path is its number of edges, which is one less than its number of vertices.
A directed edge `u → v` also gives an edge `v → u`.
In a directed graph, the in-degrees and the out-degrees each sum to `|E|`.
A simple undirected graph on `n` vertices has at most `n(n−1)/2` edges.
9.e: Count edges, and remember that direction matters.
w: True: Count the steps between vertices, not the vertices.
False: A directed edge allows travel in one direction only.
True: Every edge adds one to a single in-degree and one to a single out-degree.
False: Vertex B repeats, so the path is not simple.
True: Every unordered pair of distinct vertices can hold one edge.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about graph representations is/are true?
o: An adjacency list uses `O(V + E)` space.
With a matrix, testing whether edge `u → v` exists takes `O(1)`.
With a matrix, listing the neighbours of `u` takes `O(out-degree)`.
A weighted matrix should store 0 for a missing edge.
9.e: Space, edge tests and the missing-edge marker.
w: True: It stores one entry per vertex and one per edge.
True: It is an `n × n` grid, one cell per ordered pair of vertices.
True: It reads a single cell of the grid, with no scanning.
False: The whole row of `V` cells must be read, zeros included, so `O(V)`.
False: Zero can be a genuine weight, so ∞ marks "no edge".

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about BFS and DFS is/are true?
o: BFS uses a queue and visits nearer vertices first.
In an unweighted graph, BFS finds a fewest-edge path to each vertex when first discovered.
BFS always minimises total weight on weighted graphs.
DFS follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking.
9.e: Queue and layers against stack and depth.
w: True: A FIFO container delivers layer by layer order.
True: Earlier layers are exactly the fewer-edge vertices.
False: BFS ignores weights, so it minimises edge count only.
True: It backs up only when stuck.
False: DFS gives no guarantee about path length.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about traversal running time and conventions is/are true?
o: A traversal with adjacency lists runs in `O(V + E)`.
A traversal with an adjacency matrix runs in `O(V²)`.
A traversal with adjacency lists costs `O(V × E)`.
Under the Week 9 convention, stack DFS pushes neighbours in reverse list order.
Marking BFS vertices only when dequeued is harmless.
9.e: Lists add, matrices square, and conventions matter.
w: True: Each vertex is visited once and each adjacency entry checked once.
True: Reading a row costs `V` for each of `V` vertices.
False: The edge checks are shared across vertices, so they add rather than multiply.
True: The first-listed neighbour then ends on top and is explored first.
False: Shared vertices may be queued twice, so mark on enqueue.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about topological sorting is/are true?
o: A topological ordering lists every vertex once so that each edge `u → v` has `u` first.
Every DAG has at least one topological ordering.
A graph with a cycle has exactly one ordering.
The ordering of a DAG is always unique.
The DFS method pushes each vertex when its call finishes, then pops for the order.
9.e: Orderings exist exactly for DAGs and need not be unique.
w: True: All edges point forward in the ordering.
True: The first vertex has in-degree 0, and the rest follow.
False: A cycle makes dependencies contradictory, so there is none.
False: The course DAG has both `A, B, E, C, D, F` and `A, B, C, E, D, F`.
True: When a call finishes, everything that must come after it has already finished.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about state-space search is/are true?
o: A state describes a complete situation, such as who stands on the starting bank.
Edges represent legal moves between states.
Repeated states are worth re-exploring because they may lead somewhere new.
Invalid states, such as the wolf and goat left together without the farmer, are not expanded.
The aim is to find a sequence of actions that leads to a goal state.
10.e: States, moves, invalid and repeated states.
w: True: Vertices of the search graph are such situations.
True: Each move changes one state into another.
False: A state already seen leads to the same successors, so exploring it again only loops.
True: They break the problem's rules, so no legal plan passes through them.
True: That sequence is a path in the state graph.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about uniform cost search is/are true?
o: It expands the vertex with the least total cost from the start so far.
It keeps its candidates in a priority queue ordered by path cost.
It stops as soon as the target is first enqueued.
A queued vertex reached more cheaply keeps only the cheaper entry.
It guarantees the lowest total weight even with negative weights.
10.e: Priority by cost, update rule, stop on dequeue.
w: True: This is the definition of the strategy.
True: A smaller cost means a higher priority.
False: A cheaper path might still exist, so it stops when the target is dequeued.
True: The update rule replaces the older cost and from-vertex.
False: The guarantee needs non-negative weights.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) comparing BFS, DFS and UCS is/are true?
o: BFS uses a queue, DFS a stack and UCS a priority queue.
UCS uses edge weights, while BFS and DFS ignore them.
BFS guarantees the lowest total weight on weighted graphs.
UCS guarantees the lowest total weight when weights are non-negative.
w: True: The frontier container decides the strategy.
False: DFS gives no guarantee about path length.
True: Only UCS orders its frontier by accumulated weight.
False: BFS minimises edges, not weight.
True: The dequeued vertex cannot be improved by any frontier path.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about hops and total weight is/are true?
o: The fewest-edge route and the cheapest route can differ.
With edges S→A 2, S→B 6, S→T 9, A→B 1, A→T 8, B→T 2, the route S→T has 1 edge and weight 9.
In that graph, S→A→B→T has weight 5.
A route with fewer edges always has lower total weight.
BFS on that weighted graph returns the cheapest route.
10.e: Sum weights separately from counting edges.
w: True: Weights can make a longer route cheaper.
True: It is a single edge of weight 9.
True: `2 + 1 + 2 = 5`, the cheapest route.
False: The direct 1-edge route costs 9, more than the 3-edge route at 5.
False: BFS returns the fewest-edge route S→T, which costs 9.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the UCS trace from A to F in the example graph is/are true?
o: B's cost is updated from 0.9 to 0.4 via D.
The cheapest path is A→C→D→F with cost 1.0.
F is dequeued at step 3, when it is first enqueued.
After step 2 the queue holds B(0.9, A) and D(0.2, C).
The search stops at step 4 when E is enqueued.
w: True: The path A→C→D→B costs `0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.4`.
True: The edge costs along A→C, C→D and D→F are 0.1, 0.1 and 0.8, summing to 1.0.
False: F is first enqueued at step 3 but dequeued at step 6.
True: C was dequeued and D discovered at cost 0.2.
False: It stops when the target F is dequeued, not when another vertex is enqueued.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about counting TSP tours is/are true?
o: A round trip with symmetric distances has `(n−1)!/2` tours.
A round trip with asymmetric distances has `(n−1)!` tours.
An open path with symmetric distances has `n!` tours.
Five cities give 12 distinct symmetric round trips.
The `n!` orderings of cities each count a distinct tour once.
11.e: Divide by `n` for the start and 2 for direction when applicable.
w: True: Divide the `n!` orderings by `n` start cities and by 2 for direction.
True: A tour and its reverse now differ, so there is no division by 2.
False: A path equals its reverse, so the count is `n!/2`.
True: For five cities, `(5 − 1)!/2 = 4!/2 = 12` tours.
False: Each tour is a cycle that appears `n` times, once for each starting city.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the trade-offs of TSP strategies is/are true?
o: Random search guarantees an optimal tour.
Heuristics are fast and general but not guaranteed optimal.
Methods that are both general and optimal are fast.
11.e: Pick two of general, optimal and fast.
w: True: It evaluates all `(n−1)!/2` tours.
True: Each of the `k` tours takes `O(n)` to score.
False: It finds the optimum only by chance, closer as `k` grows.
True: They give up optimality to keep speed and generality.
False: General and optimal methods, such as brute force, are very slow.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about nearest neighbour is/are true?
o: From Belfast in the Ireland example it gives 985 km against an optimum of 940 km.
It looks ahead to the closing edge back to the start.
A tie should be broken without saying how.
It has a complete solution only after the last city is added.
w: True: It takes `n − 1` steps, each scanning up to `n` cities.
True: The tour `Belfast, Dublin, Limerick, Cork, Galway` totals 985 km.
False: It never does, so the forced last leg can be long.
False: You should state how ties were broken, since the choice can change the tour.
True: A greedy method constructs a solution piece by piece.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about local search and 2-opt is/are true?
o: Local search starts from a complete solution.
Local search can end at a local optimum that is not the global optimum.
2-opt deletes 2 edges and reconnects the pieces into a different valid tour.
The 2-opt neighbourhood has `n(n−3)/2` tours, which is `O(n²)`.
Local search always reaches the global optimum if given enough time.
11.e: Start complete, improve, stop at a local optimum.
w: True: It improves a solution that already exists, unlike greedy construction.
True: No small modification helps there, though a better solution exists elsewhere.
True: That reconnection amounts to reversing a segment.
True: The second edge may not share a city with the first, and each pair is counted twice.
False: It can stay stuck at a local optimum, however long it runs.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about greedy algorithms beyond TSP is/are true?
o: With coins 100, 60, 35, 5, 1, greedy gives 3 coins for 70 while 35 + 35 uses 2.
Greedy is always optimal for coin change.
In the 7 kg knapsack case, value-per-weight greedy takes E then D ($11), while B + E gives $14.
In the tree example, greedy gives 50 while the best path gives 91.
Greedy fails because it looks too far ahead.
11.e: Locally best is not always globally best.
w: True: The large early coin 60 leaves a remainder needing small coins.
False: This coin system is a counterexample.
True: After E and D, item B no longer fits.
True: Greedy rejects the child 2 before seeing the 67 beneath it.
False: It fails because it commits to the locally best choice without seeing the consequences.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about efficiency and tractability is/are true?
o: An efficient algorithm runs in polynomial time or lower, `O(nᵏ)`.
Exponential and factorial algorithms are inefficient.
A problem is tractable if a polynomial-time solution is known.
A problem with only exponential-time algorithms known is tractable.
At one operation per nanosecond, `O(n!)` with `n = 20` takes about 77 years.
12.e: Polynomial is efficient; a known polynomial solution makes a problem tractable.
w: True: This is the course definition of efficient.
True: `O(kⁿ)` and `O(n!)` are the inefficient classes.
True: Tractability depends on a known polynomial or better solution.
False: With no known polynomial-time solution it is intractable.
True: The table gives 77.1 years for `n = 20`.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about solving and verifying is/are true?
o: Brute-force subset sum tries `2ⁿ` subsets and costs `O(2ⁿ × n)`.
Given two factors, checking them needs a long search.
Multiplying two numbers is as hard as factoring their product.
12.e: Verification is cheap while solving is expensive.
w: True: Each of the `2ⁿ` subsets is summed in `O(n)`.
True: Add its elements and compare with 0.
False: It needs a single multiplication.
True: The elements 5, −1 and −4 add up to `5 − 1 − 4 = 0`.
False: Multiplication is easy while factoring needs a search, essentially brute force.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about P and NP is/are true?
o: P contains problems solved in polynomial time by a known algorithm.
NP contains problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time.
P ⊆ NP, because a solver can be used to verify an answer.
Every NP problem is known to be solvable in polynomial time.
12.e: P solves, NP verifies, and P is inside NP.
w: True: Sorting and multiplication are examples.
True: Subset sum and factorisation are examples.
False: It stands for non-deterministic polynomial.
True: Solve in polynomial time, then compare with the proposed answer.
False: Whether every NP problem is in P is the open P = NP question.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about reductions and NP-completeness is/are true?
o: A reduction converts any instance of problem 1 into an instance of problem 2.
If problem 1 reduces to problem 2, an algorithm for problem 2 also solves problem 1.
Subtraction reduces to addition by computing `A + (−B)`.
NP-complete problems are the intersection of NP-hard and NP.
Subset sum and SAT are NP-hard but outside NP.
12.e: Reductions transfer solvers; NP-complete is NP-hard and in NP.
w: True: This shows problem 1 is a special case of problem 2.
True: Problem 1 is therefore no harder than problem 2.
True: Negate the second number, then call any addition algorithm.
True: They are NP-hard and also in NP.
False: They are NP-complete, so they are in NP.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about NP-hardness and P = NP is/are true?
o: Optimisation TSP is NP-hard because a tour cannot easily be checked to be shortest.
Minimum graph colouring is solvable in polynomial time.
P = NP has been proven false.
If P = NP, much cryptography such as RSA would collapse.
If P ≠ NP, approximations and heuristics remain necessary for NP-complete problems.
12.e: NP-hardness, cryptography and the open question.
w: True: Checking optimality is as hard as solving the problem.
False: It is a standard NP-hard problem, not a known polynomial one.
False: Most computer scientists believe P ≠ NP, but it is unproven.
True: It relies on problems being hard to solve but easy to check.
True: No polynomial-time exact solver would exist.

1.q: Which rule multiplies the ways of every stage when all stages are needed for one outcome?
1.e: Each outcome takes one choice from every stage, so the counts multiply.
w: The sum rule adds separate cases of which only one is chosen.
The complement rule subtracts unwanted outcomes from all outcomes.
Pigeonhole guarantees a repeated category; it does not count outcomes.

1.q: Which formula counts ordered selections of `r` objects from `n` distinct objects?
1.e: This is `P(n, r)`: the product of `r` shrinking choices.
w: This divides out the `r!` internal orders, so it counts unordered selections.
This allows repetition, so the choices do not shrink.
This counts circular arrangements of all `n` objects, not ordered selections.

1.q: Which method treats objects that must stay together as one unit?
1.e: The required objects form a block, which is then multiplied by its internal arrangements.
w: The gap method keeps objects apart by placing them in gaps.
The complement rule subtracts unwanted outcomes and does not merge objects.
This method counts seatings around a table with identical rotations.

1.q: How many ways can 6 distinct objects be arranged in a line?
w: `6²` lets one object fill two positions, but each object is used once.
`5!` is the circular count `(n−1)!`, not the count for a line.
This is not a product of shrinking choices; every position still needs a choice.

1.q: How many arrangements of 5 distinct people around a round table exist when rotations are identical and reflections count as different?
w: `5!` treats rotations as different seatings.
Dividing by 2 would also identify reflections, which this question keeps different.
`5²` has no counting basis here and ignores that each person sits once.

2.q: Which complexity class has the bound `O(n log n)`?
2.e: `n` work at each of about `log n` levels gives `n log n`, as in merge sort.
w: Logarithmic is `O(log n)`, which has no factor of `n`.
Linear is `O(n)`, which has no logarithmic factor.
Exponential has the form `O(kⁿ)`, with `n` in the exponent.

o: The exact running time in seconds
An upper bound on how the operation count grows with input size
Only the memory an algorithm uses
2.e: It captures the shape of growth, not an exact count.
w: Seconds depend on hardware and language, which Big-O ignores.
Big-O can bound time or space, but it describes growth, not memory alone.
The course default is the worst case, though it can bound any case.

2.e: The dominant quadratic term decides the growth.
w: The `5n` term is smaller than `n²` for large `n`, so it cannot be the dominant term.
Lower-order terms are dropped as well, not only the constant.
Constants do not dominate; the growing terms do.

2.q: About how many iterations does a loop run when its index is halved with `i = i // 2` from `n` down to 1?
2.e: Each pass removes half of the remaining range.
w: A loop that adds 1 each pass runs `n` times, not one that halves.
A step of 2 gives `n/2`; halving the index is much faster.
A single loop cannot exceed its range, so `n²` is impossible.

2.q: Which case does the course use by default when quoting a Big-O bound?
2.e: It is a dependable upper limit on the work.
w: The best case is a special, non-representative situation.
It needs a stated input distribution, which is usually unknown.
Amortised time averages a sequence of operations; it is not the default for a single run.

3.q: Which precondition does binary search need?
o: The array must have no duplicates
The array length must be a power of 2
The key must be at the end
3.e: Sorted order lets each comparison discard half the region.
w: Duplicates do not break the halving argument.
The region can have any length; the halving just rounds.
No position is required; the search finds the key anywhere.

3.q: What is the name for a fact that stays true before and after every iteration of a loop?
3.e: It is the property that justifies correctness.
w: The stopping rule says when the loop ends, not what stays true.
State is the set of variables describing the current situation.
Progress is what changes in one iteration.

3.q: What is the worst-case complexity of insertion sort?
3.e: A reverse-ordered array forces about `n(n−1)/2` comparisons.
w: This is the bound of merge sort, not insertion sort.
This is the best case, on an already sorted array.
This is the worst case of binary search, not of sorting.

3.q: What is the time complexity of bottom-up merge sort?
w: This is the insertion sort worst case; merge sort halves the work per level.
Merging is linear per level, but there are `log₂ n` levels.
Every element must be moved at least once, so the work is at least linear.

3.q: How does the group size change from one level of bottom-up merge sort to the next?
3.e: Two neighbouring sorted groups merge into one group twice the size.
w: Halving describes top-down splitting, not bottom-up merging.
Increasing by 1 would need about `n` levels instead of `log₂ n`.
If the size never grew, the array would never become one sorted group.

4.q: Which part of a recursive function states in one sentence what `f(input)` returns?
4.e: It fixes the meaning of the function so each smaller call can be trusted.
w: The base case is the smallest input answered directly.
The reduction step shrinks the problem.
The combination step builds the current answer from the smaller one.

4.q: What is the base case of a recursive function?
o: The input that makes the most calls
The step that shrinks the problem
The value returned by the first call
The smallest input answered directly, without a recursive call
4.e: It is where the chain of calls stops.
w: The base case makes none; it ends the chain.
That is the reduction step.
The first call returns the final answer, not the base value.

4.q: What is the complexity of `T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n)`?
w: This would need constant local work, not `O(n)` per call.
Reducing `n` by 1 gives `n` levels, not `log n`.
No halving occurs here, so no `log n` factor appears.

o: The total number of calls made
The longest chain of simultaneously unfinished calls
4.e: It determines how many stack frames exist at once.
w: A branching function makes many more calls than its depth.
The depth counts nested calls, not base cases.
Return statements do not measure how deep the calls nest.

4.q: How many base cases does Fibonacci need?
w: With only one base case, the `n−2` call would miss it.
Without a base case the recursion would never stop.
Two are enough; a third is never reached by the reduction.

5.q: Which order does a stack follow?
5.e: Only the most recently added item is accessible.
w: That is the order of a queue.
A stack ignores values; only position decides.
A stack is fully determined by the order of pushes.

5.q: Which operation removes and returns the head of a queue?
5.e: It removes the earliest added item still present.
w: `enqueue` adds an item at the tail.
`peek` inspects the head without removing it.
`push` is a stack operation, not a queue operation.

5.q: What is the cost of `dequeue` in a plain array queue with the head at index 0?
5.e: Every remaining item shifts down by one index.
w: `O(1)` holds only when nothing has to shift, which is not the case at the head.
No halving occurs; the shift touches every item.
A single shift is one pass, not a nested pass.

5.q: What does `dequeue` return in a priority queue?
o: The item with the best priority
5.e: Arrival order does not decide which item leaves.
w: That describes a first-in, first-out queue.
That describes a stack, where the newest item leaves first.
Priority direction is chosen by the user; it need not be the largest.

5.q: Which end of a list should hold the stack top for `O(1)` push and pop?
5.e: Appending and popping at the end shifts no items.
w: Every push and pop would shift all other items.
The middle position is not the accessible end of the structure.
The two ends differ because the front forces shifting.

6.q: Which node of a tree has no children?
6.e: A leaf is a node with no children.
w: The root is the topmost node, which can have children.
A sibling shares a parent; it is a relationship, not a lack of children.
An ancestor is above a node in a chain of parents.

6.q: Which traversal visits the parent before either of its subtrees?
w: Inorder visits the parent between its subtrees.
Postorder visits the parent after its subtrees.
It descends a single path and is not a traversal of every node.

6.q: Which traversal of a BST visits the keys in ascending order?
6.e: It visits the left subtree, then the parent, then the right subtree.
w: Preorder starts with the root, which is not the smallest key.
Postorder ends with the root, which is not the largest key.
Inorder always sorts a BST, because of its ordering property.

6.q: What is the worst-case complexity of searching a BST with `n` nodes?
6.e: A skewed tree has height `n`, and search costs the height.
w: This holds only when the tree is balanced.
Search must descend the tree, so the cost cannot be constant.
A single search descends one path, so no `log n` factor multiplies `n`.

6.q: Which binary tree shape requires every node to have exactly 0 or 2 children?
6.e: No node has exactly one child.
w: Complete concerns how levels fill, not child counts.
Perfect additionally requires all leaves at one depth.
Height-balanced concerns subtree heights, not child counts.

7.q: Which two rules define a min-heap?
o: Left subtree < node < right subtree, with no shape rule
Perfect shape and sorted array order
Every node has 0 or 2 children and the leaves are sorted
Complete shape and every parent ≤ its children
7.e: The shape rule keeps height logarithmic and the order rule puts the minimum at the root.
w: That is the binary search tree rule, not the heap rule.
A heap need not be perfect and the array is not fully sorted.
That describes a full tree; it is not the heap rule.

7.q: Where is the minimum key in a min-heap?
o: In the middle of the array
7.e: Every path going down never decreases, so the root is smallest.
w: Leaves are the largest keys on their paths, not the smallest.
The last position is just the most recently placed leaf.
No middle position is special in a heap.

7.q: In a 0-based array heap, where is the left child of index `j`?
7.e: Levels are stored consecutively, so this index follows from doubling.
w: This is the 1-based formula, not the 0-based one.
This is the next array position, not the child.
This is the right child, not the left.

7.q: What is the time complexity of BuildHeap on `n` entries?
7.e: Most nodes are near the leaves and fall only a short way.
w: This is the cost of `n` separate insertions.
Every entry must be touched, so at least `n` work is needed.
No nested pass over all pairs occurs.

7.q: Which sorting algorithm results from using a heap-based priority queue?
7.e: Both phases cost `O(log n)` per item, giving `O(n log n)`.
w: Selection sort comes from an unsorted-list queue.
Insertion sort comes from a sorted-list queue.
Merge sort does not use a priority queue.

8.q: What does a hash function compute?
o: The row of the table where a key belongs
The sorted position of the key
How many times the key occurs
A new random row on every call
8.e: It maps a key to a row number in `0 … N−1`.
w: Hashing scatters keys and does not preserve order.
Counting occurrences is a different task.
The function must be deterministic.

8.q: What is a collision in a hash table?
o: A key that cannot be found
Two different keys hashing to the same row
8.e: Both want the same position and need a strategy to resolve it.
w: Keys are unique, so a repeat replaces the value.
A full table is a capacity issue, not a collision.
A missing key is an unsuccessful lookup, not a collision.

8.q: What is the load factor of a hash table with `n` entries and `N` rows?
8.e: It is the average number of entries per row.
w: This is the inverse: rows per entry.
A difference of counts is not a ratio of load.
This would be the fraction of spare capacity, not the load.

8.q: Which strategy places a colliding key in the next free row of the main array?
8.e: The probe moves forward, wrapping with `% N`.
w: Chaining puts the key into the bucket list of the same row.
Binary search is a search algorithm, not a collision strategy.
A traversal visits tree nodes; it does not resolve collisions.

8.q: Why does linear probing leave a deletion marker?
o: So later lookups continue past the row
To speed up insertion into empty rows
8.e: An empty row would make a lookup stop too early.
w: The marker keeps the row in use, so no memory is freed.
Insertion does not depend on the marker for speed.
Hash tables do not keep keys in order.

9.q: Which data structure does BFS use to hold vertices waiting to be explored?
9.e: A FIFO container delivers nearest-first order.
w: A stack gives depth-first order.
That is used by uniform cost search, not BFS.
A BST is not used as the BFS frontier.

9.q: What is the length of a path measured in?
o: The sum of the edge weights
9.e: It is one less than the number of vertices on the path.
w: That would be one more than the length.
That is the path's total weight, a different measure.
A path does not count cycles.

9.q: What is the running time of BFS or DFS with adjacency lists?
9.e: Each vertex is visited once and each adjacency entry checked once.
w: That is the cost with an adjacency matrix.
The edge checks add across vertices; they do not multiply.
Every vertex may need visiting, so the cost is at least linear.

9.q: What is a directed acyclic graph?
o: An undirected graph with no cycles
A directed graph in which every vertex has in-degree 0
A directed graph with no cycles
A graph in which every edge has a weight
9.e: It is the kind of graph that has a topological ordering.
w: A DAG has directed edges.
This would leave no edges at all.
Weights do not define a DAG.

9.q: Which ordering lists every vertex so that every edge points forward?
9.e: It requires `u` before `v` for every edge `u → v`.
w: BFS visits by layers and need not respect edge direction.
Inorder is a tree traversal, not a graph ordering.
Preorder is a tree traversal, not an ordering of dependencies.

10.q: Which container does uniform cost search use for its frontier?
10.e: Priority is the total path cost from the start.
w: A plain queue is the BFS frontier.
A stack is the DFS frontier.
A hash table does not order the frontier by cost.

10.q: When does uniform cost search stop?
o: When the target is first enqueued
When the queue first has two entries
10.e: Only then is its cost guaranteed to be the lowest.
w: A cheaper path might still be found.
The queue size has no relation to the target.
UCS can stop earlier, at the target.

10.q: Which strategy guarantees the lowest total weight when weights are non-negative?
10.e: It always expands the cheapest path so far.
w: It minimises edges, not weight.
It gives no guarantee about path length.
It orders a DAG and does not search for paths.

10.q: In state-space search, what does an edge represent?
o: A weight that must be summed
A legal move from one state to another
10.e: Following edges builds a sequence of actions.
w: Weights label edges but are not what an edge is.
A goal is a vertex, not an edge.
Invalid states are excluded vertices, not edges.

10.q: What is the priority of an entry in the UCS priority queue?
o: The number of edges from the start
An estimate of the remaining distance to the goal
The total path cost from the start so far
The alphabetical order of the vertex
10.e: A smaller cost means higher priority.
w: That is the BFS measure, not UCS.
That is the idea of informed search, not UCS.
Labels do not decide cost.

11.q: How many distinct round-trip tours exist for `n` cities with symmetric distances?
11.e: Divide `n!` by `n` start cities and by 2 for direction.
w: This counts every ordering, including the same tour from different starts.
This is the count when distances are asymmetric.
This is the count for an open path, not a round trip.

11.q: What is the complexity of exhaustive search for TSP?
w: This is the cost of nearest neighbour.
The number of tours grows faster than `2ⁿ`.
This is the cost of random search over `k` tours.

11.q: Which strategy always travels to the nearest unvisited city?
11.e: It makes the locally cheapest choice at every step.
w: Exhaustive search checks every tour.
Random search scores randomly chosen tours.
2-opt modifies an existing tour by exchanging edges.

11.q: What does 2-opt do to a tour?
o: Deletes 2 edges and reconnects the pieces
Builds a tour city by city
11.e: The result is a different valid tour.
w: That describes greedy construction.
That describes exhaustive search.
That describes random search.

o: A solution that no small modification improves
11.e: Local search stops there, even if a better solution exists elsewhere.
w: That is the global optimum.
The first solution need not be locally optimal.
Ties are unrelated to optimality.

o: Problems with a known polynomial-time solving algorithm
Problems that can only be verified quickly
All problems that are hard to solve
Problems solvable only in exponential time
w: That describes NP, which also contains P.
P is the efficiently solvable class, not the hard one.
Such problems are outside the known polynomial class.

12.e: It concerns polynomial-time verification of a proposed answer.
w: This is a common misreading; NP includes all of P.
The letters are not an abbreviation for this.
The letters are not an abbreviation for this.

12.q: Which relationship between P and NP is known to hold?
12.e: A solver can verify an answer by solving and comparing.
w: This would mean every verifiable problem is solvable efficiently, which is unproven.
Equality is the open question; it is unproven.
P lies inside NP, so the intersection is all of P.

12.q: What does it mean to reduce problem 1 to problem 2?
o: Convert any instance of problem 1 into an instance of problem 2
Remove constants from the Big-O of problem 1
12.e: An algorithm for problem 2 then solves problem 1.
w: The number of inputs is unrelated to a reduction.
That is simplification of Big-O, not a reduction.
Brute force is a different strategy and needs no conversion.

12.q: How is the class NP-complete defined in terms of other classes?
12.e: It is both NP-hard and in NP.
w: This would include easy problems in P.
This is just P, which is not hard.
Without membership in NP, a problem is merely NP-hard.

lessons.title: Counting
lessons.goal: Count how many valid outcomes a problem allows, using a small set of rules.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Counting gives the arithmetic behind "how much work?". Later chapters count loop iterations, tours and orderings.
🧠 Memory hook
One outcome first. Describe a single valid outcome, then ask: AND or OR? Order? Repetition?
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
What a counting question asksProduct rule (AND)Sum rule (OR)Inclusion–exclusion (overlapping OR)Complement and pigeonholePermutations (order matters)Combinations (order does not matter)Block method (objects stay together)Gap method (objects stay apart)Circular arrangementsWording guide
⚡ At a glance — the counting toolkit
Product rule (AND)Sum rule (OR)Inclusion–exclusionComplementPermutationCombinationBlockGapCircular
1.1What a counting question asks

W1 · A.1

Every counting question asks how many different valid outcomes exist. Before using any formula, describe what one complete outcome looks like.

Three questions control almost every solution:

  • Are we completing several required stages (AND) or choosing one of several separate cases (OR)?
  • Does order matter?
  • Is repetition allowed?

Seven-step method

  • Define one outcome.
  • List the restrictions: underline "different", "at least", "exactly", "together", "not adjacent".
  • Decide AND (multiply) or OR (add).
  • Decide whether order matters.
  • Decide whether repetition is allowed.
  • Handle restrictions by direct counting, cases, complement, block or gaps.
  • Write a labelled formula, calculate, then sanity-check.
1.2Product rule (AND)

W1 · A.2

If task 1 can be done in m ways and task 2 in n ways, and both are needed, there are m × n ways to do both.

  • Binary strings of length n: each position has 2 choices and every position is needed, so 2ⁿ.
  • Arranging n distinct objects: n × (n−1) × ⋯ × 1 = n!, because each filled position leaves one fewer choice.

Three-letter codes from {A, B, C, D, E} with no repeats are 5 × 4 × 3 = 60, not 5³. The formula 5³ allows repeats such as AAA.

1.3Sum rule (OR)

W1 · A.3

If task 1 can be done in m ways or task 2 in n ways, and the cases cannot happen together, there are m + n ways to do exactly one of them.

SignalMeaningOperation
All stages needed to build one outcomeANDMultiply
One case chosen from separate possibilitiesORAdd

Do not trust the English word alone. Trace how one complete outcome is built.

1.4Inclusion–exclusion (overlapping OR)

W1 · A.4

When two cases can happen at the same time, plain addition counts the overlap twice: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.

Integers 1–1000 divisible by 3 or 5: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467. The 66 multiples of 15 were counted in both lists.

1.5Complement and pigeonhole

W1 · A.5

Complement rule: wanted = all − unwanted. For "at least one", count the outcomes with none.

Four-character passwords from 36 symbols (A–Z, 0–9) with at least one digit: 36⁴ − 26⁴ = 1,222,640.

Pigeonhole principle: with more objects than categories, some category holds more than one. To guarantee m objects in one of k categories you need k(m−1) + 1 objects. Two students sharing a birth month needs 12 + 1 = 13.

1.6Permutations (order matters)

W1 · A.6

An ordered arrangement of r of n distinct objects: P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!.

Filling r positions left to right leaves n, n−1, …, n−r+1 choices, all needed, so the product is n!/(n−r)!. Awarding gold, silver and bronze among 150 entrants: 150 × 149 × 148 = 3,307,800.

Swap test. If swapping two chosen items gives a different valid outcome, use a permutation.

1.7Combinations (order does not matter)

W1 · A.7

An unordered selection of r of n objects: C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!) = P(n, r)/r!.

Each unordered group appears r! times in the ordered count, so dividing by r! removes the overcounting. Choosing 3 of 150 with ranking ignored: 3,307,800 / 6 = 551,300.

1.8Block method (objects stay together)

W1 · A.8

  • Merge the k required objects into one block, giving n − k + 1 outside objects.
  • Arrange the outside objects: (n − k + 1)!.
  • Arrange inside the block: k!.
  • Multiply.

Six distinct people in a row, two of them adjacent: 5! × 2! = 240.

Forgetting the internal factor k! assumes the block has only one internal order.

1.9Gap method (objects stay apart)

W1 · A.9

  • Arrange the m ordinary objects first. They create m + 1 gaps.
  • Choose gaps for the special objects: C(m+1, k).
  • Arrange the k special objects if they are distinct: k!.

Three men and three women in a line, no two women adjacent: 3! × C(4,3) × 3! = 144. If more than m + 1 special objects must be pairwise apart, the count is 0.

1.10Circular arrangements

W1 · A.10

For n distinct people at a round table, with rotations identical, the count is (n − 1)!. Fix one person, then arrange the rest relative to them.

If reflections are also identical (only neighbours matter), divide by 2: (n − 1)!/2 for n ≥ 3.

1.11Wording guide

W1 · A.11

Words in the questionFirst method to consider
and; followed by; one of eachProduct rule
either; one type or anotherSum rule
A or B, possibly bothInclusion–exclusion
at least one; not allComplement
arrange; rank; roles; positionsPermutation
choose; select; committee; groupCombination
must be adjacent; togetherBlock method
no two adjacent; separatedGap method
around a table; in a circleCircular arrangement
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The ten counting methods of the course.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Product ruleMultiplies the ways of every required stage.All stages are needed (AND).
Sum ruleAdds the ways of separate, mutually exclusive cases.Exactly one case is chosen (OR).
Inclusion–exclusionAdds two overlapping cases, then subtracts the overlap.Sum rule with a non-empty overlap.
Complement ruleSubtracts the unwanted outcomes from all outcomes.Signalled by "at least one" or "not".
Pigeonhole principleGuarantees a category with more than one object.Proves existence; it does not count outcomes.
PermutationCounts ordered selections, n!/(n−r)!.Swapping two items changes the outcome.
CombinationCounts unordered selections, n!/(r!(n−r)!).Swapping two items changes nothing.
Block methodGlues required-together objects into one unit.Multiplies by the internal arrangements.
Gap methodPlaces special objects into gaps between ordinary ones.Uses m + 1 gaps and C(m+1, k).
Circular arrangementCounts seatings with rotations identical, (n−1)!.Divides by n compared with a line.

Permutations and combinations are selection formulas built on the product rule. They are not separate rules.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1.1

Multiples of 3 or 5

The problem

How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by 3 or by 5?

The trace
  • Multiples of 3: ⌊1000/3⌋ = 333.
  • Multiples of 5: ⌊1000/5⌋ = 200.
  • Multiples of both, meaning of 15: ⌊1000/15⌋ = 66.
  • Total: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467.
The lesson

A number can satisfy both cases, so subtract the overlap once.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1.2

Together and apart in a circle

The problem

Six people sit at a round table. Two must sit together and two others must not sit next to each other.

The trace
  • Block the first pair: 5 circular objects give 4! = 24, times 2! inside the block, so 48.
  • Remove arrangements where the second pair is also together: 4 circular objects give 3! = 6, times 2! × 2!, so 24.
  • Valid arrangements: 48 − 24 = 24.
The lesson

Count the requirement first, then subtract the unwanted overlap inside it.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Licence plates. A plate begins with S, followed by two uppercase letters, four digits and one uppercase letter. How many plates are possible?
Show answer
Product rule over eight positions: 1 · 26 · 26 · 10⁴ · 26 = 26³ · 10⁴ = 175,760,000.
2
Non-taxi plates. Plates beginning with SH are reserved for taxis. How many plates remain for non-taxis?
Show answer
Subtract the reserved set: 26³·10⁴ − 26²·10⁴ = 169,000,000. With S and H fixed, one letter, four digits and a final letter vary.
3
Passwords with at least one digit. How many case-insensitive alphanumeric passwords of length 6, 7 or 8 contain at least one digit?
Show answer
Complement rule for each length k: 36ᵏ − 26ᵏ (all strings minus letters only). The lengths are mutually exclusive, so add: (36⁶−26⁶)+(36⁷−26⁷)+(36⁸−26⁸) = 2,684,483,063,360.
4
Starts with a or ends with z. Using lowercase letters and digits, how many 6-character passwords start with a or end with z?
Show answer
Inclusion–exclusion: |A| = 36⁵, |Z| = 36⁵, |A ∩ Z| = 36⁴, so 36⁵ + 36⁵ − 36⁴ = 119,252,736.
5
Keeping A, B and C together. How many permutations of A to H keep ABC consecutive? What if A, B and C stay together in any internal order?
Show answer
Treat the three letters as one block, giving six objects. Exactly ABC: 6! = 720. Any internal order: 6! · 3! = 4,320.
6
Four diners, six seats. Four diners occupy four of six distinct seats. How many seating arrangements are there?
Show answer
Order matters: P(6,4) = 6!/2! = 360. Equivalently choose then arrange: C(6,4) · 4! = 15 · 24 = 360.
7
Forming the committee. How many 7-member committees contain 3 faculty chosen from 40 and 4 students chosen from 300?
Show answer
Two independent selections, so the product rule gives C(40,3) · C(300,4) = 3,268,216,809,000.
8
No two women adjacent. How many ways can 3 men and 3 women stand in a line if no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Arrange the men (3!), which creates 4 gaps. Choose 3 of the 4 gaps and arrange the women: 3! · C(4,3) · 3! = 6 · 4 · 6 = 144, which equals 3! · P(4,3).
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Multiple-choice test (Rosen 6.1 Q3). A test has 10 questions with 4 possible answers each. In how many ways can a student answer if every question is answered? If blanks are allowed?
Show answer
Every question answered: 4¹⁰. Blanks allowed: each question has 5 options, so 5¹⁰.
2
Integers 100 to 999 (Rosen 6.1 Q23). How many integers from 100 to 999 inclusive: divisible by 7; odd; with three equal digits; not divisible by 4; divisible by 3 or 4; divisible by neither 3 nor 4; divisible by 3 but not 4; divisible by 3 and 4?
Show answer
In order: 128; 450; 9; 675; 450; 450; 225; 75. For example, 3 or 4: 300 + 225 − 75 = 450, and 3 and 4 means divisible by 12, which gives 75.
3
Two licence plate formats (Rosen 6.1 Q29). How many plates can be made from either 2 letters then 4 digits, or 2 digits then 4 letters?
Show answer
Sum rule over two disjoint formats: 26²·10⁴ + 10²·26⁴ = 52,457,600.
4
Circular seating, neighbours only (Rosen 6.1 Q45). Seat six people around a circular table where two seatings are the same if everyone has the same two neighbours, ignoring left and right.
Show answer
5!/2 = 60: fix one person to remove rotations, then halve to ignore reflections.
5
Wedding photograph (Rosen 6.1 Q47). Six people stand in a row, including the bride and groom. How many ways if the bride must be next to the groom; not next to the groom; to the left of the groom?
Show answer
Next to each other: block method 5! · 2 = 240. Not next to: 720 − 240 = 480. Bride somewhere left of the groom: half of all orders, 720/2 = 360.
6
Permutations ending in a (Rosen 6.3 Q3). How many permutations of {a, b, c, d, e, f, g} end with a?
Show answer
Fix the last letter and arrange the other six: 6! = 720.
7
Alternating men and women (Rosen 6.3 Q13). A group has n men and n women. In how many ways can they stand in a row if men and women alternate?
Show answer
Choose which sex starts (2 ways), then arrange each sex: 2 · (n!)².
8
Ten coin flips (Rosen 6.3 Q19). A coin is flipped 10 times. How many outcomes are there in total, with exactly two heads, with at most three tails, and with equal heads and tails?
Show answer
Total 2¹⁰ = 1,024. Exactly two heads C(10,2) = 45. At most three tails C(10,0)+C(10,1)+C(10,2)+C(10,3) = 176. Equal heads and tails C(10,5) = 252.
9
8 men and 5 women, no two women adjacent (Rosen 6.3 Q23). How many ways can 8 men and 5 women stand in a line so that no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Place the men first (8!), which creates 9 gaps. Place the women in gaps: P(9,5). Total 8! · P(9,5) = 609,638,400.
10
Club of 25 members (Rosen 6.3 Q27). How many ways are there to choose 4 members for an executive committee, and to choose a president, vice president, secretary and treasurer with no person holding two offices?
Show answer
Committee: order does not matter, C(25,4) = 12,650. Offices: order matters, P(25,4) = 303,600.
11
Cinema seating. 19 students occupy a row of 22 seats. How many ways? If Andrew, Brandon and Cheryl join (22 students in 22 seats) and Brandon sits at either end, how many ways?
Show answer
First part P(22,19) = 22!/3! ≈ 1.87 × 10²⁰. Second part: 2 end seats for Brandon, then the other 21 people fill 21 seats, 2 · 21! ≈ 1.02 × 10²⁰.
12
10 men and 10 women. How many ways are there to arrange them in a row? How many ways to seat all 20 at two circular tables (one blue, one red) with 5 men and 5 women alternating at each?
Show answer
Row: 20! ≈ 2.43 × 10¹⁸. Two alternating tables: (C(10,5)·C(10,5)·4!·5!/2) · (C(5,5)·C(5,5)·4!·5!/2) ≈ 1.32 × 10¹¹. The answer key says rounded values are for reference; the formula is what you must produce.
⚡ Quick examples
Permutation or combination?
PointUse the swap test on two selected items.
ExampleGold and silver swapped is a new outcome, so it is a permutation.
ExplanationA changed outcome means order matters.
Complement shortcut
Point36⁴ − 26⁴ counts passwords with at least one digit.
ExampleAll passwords minus the all-letter passwords.
ExplanationCounting "none" is far easier than counting "at least one" directly.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Describe one outcome before choosing a formula.
  • AND multiplies; separate OR cases add; overlapping OR subtracts the overlap.
  • Order matters: P(n,r). Order ignored: C(n,r) = P(n,r)/r!.
  • Together: block, times k! inside. Apart: gaps, m + 1 of them.
  • Circle with identical rotations: (n−1)!; also identical reflections: (n−1)!/2.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Product rule vs sum ruletap to flip
Multiply when every stage is needed; add when exactly one separate case is chosen.
Why divide by r! in C(n,r)?tap to flip
Each unordered group appears r! times in the ordered count.
Guarantee two in the same one of 12 categoriestap to flip
12 + 1 = 13 objects.
Number of gaps from m ordinary objectstap to flip
m + 1.
➡ Where next? Counting tells you how many inputs and operations exist. Next, Big-O uses counts to compare growth.

lessons.title: Complexity and Big-O
lessons.goal: Compare algorithms by how their work grows with input size, not by seconds.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Big-O lets you compare algorithms fairly, whatever the language, hardware or test input.
🧠 Memory hook
Count, then simplify. Count the iterations first. Drop constants and keep the dominant term last.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
What an algorithm isWhy count growth, not secondsGrowth rate and Big-OComplexity classesDominance rulesSix-step method for codeLoop patterns
⚡ At a glance — growth order, slowest-growing first
1→log n→n→n log n→n²→n³→2ⁿ→n!
2.1What an algorithm is

W2 · B.1

An algorithm is a complete specification for solving a problem. It has three parts:

  • Inputs: the data it starts with.
