  • Outputs: the answer it produces.
  • A finite sequence of simple, precise, effective steps from input to output.

The form does not matter: code, pseudocode or plain steps. What matters is the input–output contract. Knuth asks for steps that are precise (unambiguous), effective (they move towards the goal) and practical (finish in reasonable time).

Property of a good algorithmMeaning
CorrectnessRight output for every valid input
Space efficiencyUses as little memory as possible
Time efficiencyRuns as fast as possible; the focus of this chapter
2.2Why count growth, not seconds

W2 · B.2–B.4

Efficiency is not about programming language, operating system, processor speed, whose implementation it is, or the size of one test input. It is about how the number of operations grows as the input grows.

InputBrute-force gcd (iterations)Repeated-subtraction gcd (iterations)
gcd(81, 36)285
gcd(330, 231)1995
gcd(1989, 867)8178

Same input and output, very different work. Brute force is not always a real option: trying every ordering of 80 localities means 80! ≈ 7.2 × 10¹¹⁸ orderings.

2.3Growth rate and Big-O

W2 · B.5

Growth rate is how the operation count grows as n grows. Big-O such as O(n²) says that for large n the work grows roughly like n². It is an upper bound on the shape of growth, not an exact count.

State what a measurement covers before giving a bound:

TermMeaning
Best caseLeast work among valid inputs of the same size
Worst caseMost work among valid inputs of the same size; the course default
Average caseExpected work under a stated distribution of inputs
Amortised timeTotal cost of a sequence of operations divided across them; no randomness assumed
Auxiliary spaceExtra memory beyond the input that exists at the same time

Worst case is the default because the best case is a special situation, and the average case needs input frequencies we usually lack. Give the tightest bound you can justify.

2.4Complexity classes

W2 · B.6

NameBig-OTypical source
ConstantO(1)Unaffected by input size
LogarithmicO(log n)Halving, as in binary search
LinearO(n)One pass over the input
LinearithmicO(n log n)Merge sort
PolynomialO(nᵏ)k = 2 quadratic, k = 3 cubic
ExponentialO(kⁿ)k constant
FactorialO(n!)Often grouped with exponential
Big-OWhen n doubles
O(1)Operations stay the same
O(log n)Operations rise by about 1
O(n)Operations double
O(n²)Operations quadruple
O(2ⁿ)Adding 1 to n already doubles the operations
O(n!)Adding 1 to n multiplies the operations by n

A machine 1000 times faster lifts the feasible size of an n! algorithm only from about 9.5 to 12.5.

2.5Dominance rules

W2 · B.7

  • Drop constant multipliers: O(7n) = O(n).
  • Keep only the dominant term of a sum: O(n² + 5n + 20) = O(n²).
  • Multiply repeated costs: n iterations of O(n) work give O(n²).

Growth order to memorise: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.

ExpressionBoundReason
1000 · 2ⁿO(2ⁿ)A fixed multiplier
0.0001 · 2.1ⁿO(2.1ⁿ)The base is not a multiplier: 2.1ⁿ / 2ⁿ = 1.05ⁿ grows without bound
5ⁿ + 2ⁿO(5ⁿ)The larger base dominates
n! · n²O(n! · n²)Factors of a product all stay
2ᵐ + 2ⁿ, or m · nO(2ᵐ + 2ⁿ), O(mn)Independent inputs cannot be compared; keep both

Constants matter for speed, not for scaling.

2.6Six-step method for code

W2 · B.8

  • Name the input size(s): n, possibly m or k.
  • Split the code into blocks: statements, loops, conditionals, calls.
  • Count each loop's iterations exactly first: n, n/2, i, log₂ n.
  • Find the cost of one iteration, including nested loops and calls. A call is not automatically O(1).
  • Combine: multiply iterations by cost per iteration, add consecutive blocks, and use a summation when cost depends on the index.
  • Simplify only at the end.
2.7Loop patterns

W2 · B.9

PatternCost
range(n), range(10, n), range(0, n, 2)O(n): constant offsets and divisors drop out
range(20)O(1)
Consecutive loops over n then mO(n + m): add
Nested independent loops over n and mO(nm): multiply
Triangular loop, inner count iΣ i = n(n+1)/2, so O(n²)
i = i * 2 or i = i // 2About log₂ n iterations: O(log n)
Inner work about n/i for each in · Hₙ, so O(n log n)

The log base never matters: changing base only adds a constant factor, so O(log₂ n) = O(log₃ n). Careful: log(n²) = 2 log n is O(log n), but (log n)² is not.

An early-return search has a best case of O(1) and a worst case of O(n). Always state which one you mean.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The seven complexity classes, in increasing order of growth.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
ConstantO(1): work independent of n.No loop over the input.
LogarithmicO(log n): the problem shrinks by a constant factor each step.Halving loops.
LinearO(n): work proportional to n.One pass.
LinearithmicO(n log n): n work at each of log n levels.Between linear and quadratic.
PolynomialO(nᵏ) for constant k.The variable is in the base.
ExponentialO(kⁿ) for constant k.The variable is in the exponent.
FactorialO(n!).Grows faster than every kⁿ.

Quadratic and cubic are polynomial with k = 2 and k = 3. They are not separate classes.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2.1

Triangular loop

The problem

An outer loop runs i from 1 to n; the inner loop runs i times with constant work.

The trace
  • Inner iterations per i: i.
  • Total: 1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = n(n+1)/2.
  • Dominant term: n²/2; drop the constant. Result: O(n²).
The lesson

When the inner cost depends on the index, write a summation instead of multiplying.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2.2

Constant offset and divisor

The problem

Compare range(n), range(10, n) and range(0, n, 2).

The trace
  • Iterations: n, n − 10 and n/2.
  • Every one is a constant multiple or offset of n.
The lesson

Count exactly first. Constants then drop out and all three are O(n).

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Complexity of an exam-style recursion. What is the time complexity of z(n) when each call loops n times calling z(n-1)?
Show answer
T(n) = n · T(n−1), which unrolls to n!, so O(n!).
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Counting steps from a table. A table gives, for each input value, the number of times an operation is performed (the count is the input plus a constant). What is the Big O?
Show answer
O(n): the number of operations grows linearly with the input, and the constant offset is dropped.
2
Simplify the step counts. Give the Big O of: (a) 9 + 0.02N² + 0.1N, (b) N² + 2N − 3, (c) N! + 100N²⁰, (d) 2ᴺ + N!, (e) 5N log₂N + N√N, (f) N² log₂N + N (log₂N)², (h) 10⁵ + 10⁴(log N)² + 10³ log N².
Show answer
(a) O(N²); (b) O(N²); (c) O(N!); (d) O(N!); (e) O(N^1.5) because N√N beats N log N; (f) O(N² log N); (h) O((log N)²). Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constants.
3
Three loop shapes. Give the complexity of: two loops in a row over n and m; a nested n × n loop followed by a single n loop; and a loop where the inner while j > i runs from n down to i.
Show answer
Two loops in a row: O(n + m) or O(max(n, m)). Nested then single: O(n²). Dependent inner loop: n + (n−1) + … + 1, so O(n²).
4
f, g and h. f(n) sums 1..n−1 in a loop. g(n) loops i from 1 to n−1 and calls f(i) each time. h(n) returns f(n) + g(n). Give each complexity.
Show answer
f is O(n). g calls an O(i) function n times: 1 + 2 + … + n, so O(n²). h is O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²).
5
Cost of a nested call. func_a has two nested loops of size n and calls f(j) inside. What is its complexity if f costs a constant T, and if f(j) costs j time units?
Show answer
Constant T: n² · T = O(n²). Linear f(j) = j: n · (0 + 1 + … + (n−1)) = n · n(n−1)/2, which is O(n³).
6
Helper call inside loops. sub_func(n) is called inside: func_6a (for i in range(n), for j in range(i)); func_6b (for i in 1..n, for j in 1..i²); func_2c (for i, for j, if j % i == 0, for k in 1..n).
Show answer
The answer key gives O(n³), O(n⁴) and O(n³ log n), which is what you get when sub_func(n) costs O(n): 6a runs it n(n−1)/2 times; 6b runs it Σi² ≈ n³/3 times; in 2c the if is true about n/i times per i, a harmonic sum n log n, and each hit runs n calls of cost n.
⚡ Quick examples
Dominant term
PointKeep only the fastest-growing term.
Examplen log n + n simplifies to O(n log n).
ExplanationFor large n, the lower terms become negligible.
Halving loop
PointA loop that halves its index runs log₂ n times.
Examplei = i // 2 from n down to 1.
ExplanationEach iteration removes half the remaining range.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • An algorithm has inputs, outputs and finite precise, effective steps.
  • Measure growth in operations, never seconds, language or hardware.
  • Worst case is the default; state which case you give.
  • Order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.
  • Drop constant multipliers; keep the dominant term; keep independent variables.
  • Add consecutive blocks, multiply nested ones, sum when the cost depends on the index.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Which case is the default?tap to flip
Worst case.
Effect of doubling n on O(n²)tap to flip
Operations quadruple.
Why does the log base not matter?tap to flip
Changing base adds only a constant factor.
Is 0.0001 · 2.1ⁿ an O(2ⁿ) bound?tap to flip
No. The base is not a multiplier, so it is O(2.1ⁿ).
➡ Where next? You can now cost loops. Next, apply that to searching and sorting.

lessons.title: Searching and Sorting
lessons.goal: Reason about loops, then compare linear and binary search, and insertion and merge sort.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
A smarter algorithm changes the growth rate, which no faster hardware can do.
🧠 Memory hook
Halve it. Binary search and merge sort win by halving: log n steps instead of n.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Reasoning about any iterative algorithmLinear searchBinary searchLinear against binary searchInsertion sortMerge sort (bottom-up)Insertion sort against merge sort
⚡ At a glance — four algorithms
Linear search O(n)Binary search O(log n)Insertion sort O(n²)Merge sort O(n log n)
3.1Reasoning about any iterative algorithm

W3 · C.1a

A useful loop makes progress towards finishing. Ask four questions of any iterative algorithm:

  • State: which variables describe the current situation? Examples: low and high; the sorted-prefix boundary i.
  • Progress: what changes in one iteration? The region shrinks, or the sorted prefix grows by one.
  • Invariant: which fact stays true before and after every iteration? Examples: "if the key exists it lies between low and high"; "a[0:i] is sorted".
  • Stopping rule: exactly when does the loop finish?

Tracing by hand

  • Copy the input and label every index.
  • Write the initial values of the important variables.
  • Execute one iteration only.
  • Record every changed variable.
  • Check the stopping condition before the next row.
3.2Linear search

W3 · C.2

Start at the beginning and compare items one by one until the key is found or the collection ends. It returns the index, or -1 on failure.

  • Unsuccessful search: every item is checked, so n comparisons.
  • Successful search: 1 comparison at best, n at worst, and (n + 1)/2 on average.
  • Complexity: O(n). No precondition on the order.
3.3Binary search

W3 · C.3

Linear search removes one candidate per comparison. Binary search removes half, but needs a sorted array. Look at the middle item and discard the half that cannot contain the key.

python
def binary_search(a, k): # a must be sorted lower, upper = -1, len(a) # region is a[lower+1 .. upper-1] while upper > lower + 1: # region not empty mid = (lower + upper) // 2 if a[mid] == k: return mid elif k < a[mid]: upper = mid else: lower = mid return -1

Convention: lower is one index below the region and upper one above it. The region is empty exactly when upper == lower + 1, which is the failure condition.

Reducing n to 1 by halving takes m steps where 2ᵐ ≈ n, so m = log₂ n. Worst case log₂ n + 1 steps, so O(log n). Best case O(1).

3.4Linear against binary search

W3 · C.4

Linear searchBinary search
PreconditionNoneArray must be sorted
StrategyScan left to rightHalve the region each step
Best caseO(1)O(1)
Worst case, sorted arrayO(n)O(log n)
Unsorted arrayO(n)Not applicable
Comparisons for n = 15Up to 15Up to about 4

Both have an O(1) best case, so the worst case separates them.

3.5Insertion sort

W3 · D.1–D.5

The invariant is that the left part of the array is already sorted. The item being placed is the key. Slide it left past every larger item and drop it into place, like sorting a hand of cards.

python
def insertion_sort(a): for i in range(1, len(a)): # a[0:i] is already sorted key = a[i] j = i - 1 while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j + 1] = a[j] # slide larger items right j -= 1 a[j + 1] = key
  • The outer loop calls an inner loop, so insertion sort has nested loops.
  • Worst case: a strictly reverse-ordered array. Every key slides to the front, giving n(n−1)/2 potential comparisons, so O(n²).
  • Best case: an already sorted array. Each key needs one comparison, so O(n).
3.6Merge sort (bottom-up)

W3 · E.1–E.5

Merge sort applies the divide-and-conquer idea to sorting. This chapter uses the iterative, bottom-up version: start from groups of size 1 and merge neighbouring sorted groups. The group size gs doubles at each level: 1, 2, 4, 8, …

python
def merge(left, right): out, i, j = [], 0, 0 while i < len(left) and j < len(right): if left[i] <= right[j]: # tie: take from left first out.append(left[i]); i += 1 else: out.append(right[j]); j += 1 return out + left[i:] + right[j:]
  • Going from size 1 to size n takes log₂ n levels.
  • At every level, the merges together touch every element once: n elements per level.
  • Total work: n × log₂ n, so O(n log n) in the best and worst case alike.

Merging sorted lists of lengths n and m takes O(n + m): every step advances one index and never moves backwards.

3.7Insertion sort against merge sort

W3 · E.5

Insertion sortMerge sort
StrategyNested loops, slide items leftDivide and conquer, bottom-up merge
Worst caseO(n²)O(n log n)
Best caseO(n), already sortedO(n log n): always does full merges
On an already sorted arrayFewer comparisonsStill does its full n log n work

Sorting first and then doing an O(n) scan costs O(n log n) in total, because the sorting term dominates.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The four questions for any iterative algorithm.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
StateThe variables that describe where the algorithm is now.A snapshot, not a rule.
ProgressWhat changes in one iteration.A change, not a fact.
InvariantA fact true before and after every iteration.Justifies correctness.
Stopping ruleThe exact condition that ends the loop.Decides termination.

The invariant is not the stopping rule: one says what stays true, the other says when to stop.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3.1

Binary search for 57

The problem

Search [4, 10, 22, 35, 36, 57, 65, 71, 79, 83, 87, 89, 90, 91, 93] (n = 15) for 57.

The trace
Steploweruppermida[mid]Action
1−11577157 < 71, so upper = 7
2−1733557 > 35, so lower = 3
337557Found
The lesson

Three comparisons suffice for 15 items, because each one halves the region.

WORKED EXAMPLE 3.2

Merging with a tie rule

The problem

Merge A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31] and B = [4, 9, 12, 28], keeping both 9s and taking from A first on a tie.

The trace
Front valuesTakeOutput so far
2, 4A: 2[2]
9, 4B: 4[2, 4]
9, 9A: 9 (tie)[2, 4, 9]
15, 9B: 9[2, 4, 9, 9]
15, 12B: 12[2, 4, 9, 9, 12]
15, 28A: 15[2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15]
23, 28A: 23[… , 23]
31, 28B: 28[… , 28]
A endsCopy A: 31[2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]
The lesson

Taking the smaller front value is safe: both inputs are sorted, so nothing smaller can hide behind either front.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
First index with a[index] ≥ key. Correct first_at_least(a, key) so it returns the first index where a[index] ≥ key, or None. Trace keys 8, 20 and 40 on a = [3, 8, 8, 14, 19, 27, 31] and state time and space.
Show answer
Keep ans. If a[mid] >= key, save ans = mid and search left (high = mid − 1); otherwise low = mid + 1. Return ans after the loop. Results: key 8 gives index 1; key 20 gives index 5 (a[5] = 27, a[4] = 19); key 40 gives None because ans is never updated. Time O(log n), space O(1). The original bug moved right after a valid value and returned an index even when nothing qualified.
2
Run-length encoding in one pass. Convert [4, 4, 4, 7, 7, 2, 2, 2, 2, 9] into [(4, 3), (7, 2), (2, 4), (9, 1)], handling empty input and explaining the final append.
Show answer
State: value, count, out. Start value, count = a[0], 1. Equal next item: count += 1. Different: append (value, count) and restart. A run is appended only when a change is seen, so the last run must be appended once after the loop. Time O(n), working space O(1), output space O(r) for r runs.
3
Merge two sorted arrays, keeping duplicates. Merge A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31] and B = [4, 9, 12, 28], taking from A first on a tie.
Show answer
Compare A[i] with B[j]; take A[i] when A[i] <= B[j], else B[j]; advance only the index used; copy leftovers. Result [2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]. At most n + m values are appended: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) output space.
4
Count inversions with nested loops. For a = [7, 2, 6, 3, 5], compare every pair i < j and count the pairs with a[i] > a[j].
Show answer
Inner loop starts at j = i + 1 so each pair is compared once. Inversions: (7,2), (7,6), (7,3), (7,5), (6,3), (6,5), so the count is 6. Comparisons n(n−1)/2, time O(n²), working space O(1).
5
Search a row-and-column sorted matrix. Start at the top-right cell and find 13. Move left when the current value is larger than the target and down when it is smaller.
Show answer
If the current value is too large, its whole column below is larger, so move left. If it is too small, its whole row to the left is smaller, so move down. For target 13 the path is 18, 10, 15, 9, 13, found at row 2, column 1 (zero-based). Each comparison discards a row or column: at most r + c − 1 checks, O(r + c) time, O(1) space.
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Linear against binary search counts. x = [8, 9, 11, 16, 32, 37, 43, 45, 52, 55, 58, 61, 63, 66, 68, 82, 95, 99]. How many elements do linear and binary search check to find 8, 16 and 50?
Show answer
Key 8: 1 and 4. Key 16: 4 and 2. Key 50 (absent): 18 and 5.
2
Modify linear search for duplicates. Return (a) the number of occurrences of k, (b) the index of the second occurrence or None, (c) the index of the last occurrence or None.
Show answer
(a) Do not return inside the loop; keep count += 1 and return count after it. (b) Increment count on a match and return i when count == 2; otherwise None. (c) Remember the latest matching index in last_index and return it after the loop, or scan from the back and return the first match.
3
Insertion sort, descending. Change the insertion sort to sort in descending order. What are its best and worst cases?
Show answer
Change the shifting condition to while position > 0 and value > list[position-1]. Best case O(n) when the input is already in descending order. Worst case O(n²) when it is in ascending order.
4
Merge sort just before the final merge. What does x look like just before the final merge for [96, 80, 88, 34, 47, 65, 52, 73], [62, 77, 18, 48, 64, 45, 34, 88, 82, 87, 17] and [27, 92, 93, 91, 35, 22, 31]?
Show answer
The two halves are sorted and not yet merged: [34, 80, 88, 96, 47, 52, 65, 73]; [18, 34, 45, 48, 62, 64, 77, 88, 17, 82, 87]; [27, 91, 92, 93, 22, 31, 35].
5
Maximum of a shifted sorted array. A sorted array A is shifted right by k to give Aₖ. Find the maximum when k is known in O(1), when k is unknown in O(N), and when k is unknown in O(log N).
Show answer
Known k: the original maximum at index n−1 moves to ((n−1) + k) % n = (k−1) % n, so read that index in O(1). Unknown k, O(N): linear scan until an element is larger than its right neighbour. Unknown k, O(log N): binary search; if the middle element is bigger than the one to its right, it is the maximum, otherwise move toward the side that contains the break.
6
Find the missing integer. B holds n distinct integers from 1 to n + 1 with exactly one missing. Find it with the lowest complexity.
Show answer
Four approaches in the answer key: search for each number in turn, O(n²); sort then find the gap, O(n log n); compare the sum with 1 + 2 + … + (n+1), O(n) time and O(1) space; or a flag array, O(n).
⚡ Quick examples
Choosing a search
PointUse binary search only on sorted data.
ExampleSorted array of 15 items: at most about 4 comparisons.
ExplanationThe sorted order lets each comparison discard half.
Reading a sort bound
PointInsertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case and O(n) in the best.
ExampleReverse-ordered input against already sorted input.
ExplanationThe best and worst cases correspond to how far each key slides.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Ask state, progress, invariant and stopping rule of every loop.
  • Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n) but needs a sorted array.
  • Insertion sort keeps a sorted left part: O(n²) worst, O(n) best.
  • Bottom-up merge sort doubles the group size: log₂ n levels of n work, so O(n log n).
  • Merging two sorted lists costs O(n + m).
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Average comparisons of a successful linear searchtap to flip
(n + 1)/2.
Why does binary search need a sorted array?tap to flip
The order lets you discard the half that cannot contain the key.
Insertion sort best casetap to flip
O(n) on an already sorted array.

➡ Where next? Merge sort here is built with loops. Next, recursion expresses the same decomposition with self-calls.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.goal: Decompose a problem with self-calls, trace calls, and derive Big-O from a recurrence.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Recursion is a second way to decompose problems, and recurrences let you cost it exactly.
🧠 Memory hook
Calls go down, values come up. Trace in two phases, and read the recurrence from one call.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
What recursion isThree safety questionsTracing in two phasesBranching recursion: FibonacciHalving is not automatically O(log n)RecurrencesCommon mistakes
⚡ At a glance — the four parts of a recursive function
Contract→Base case→Reduction step→Combination step
4.1What recursion is

W4 · F.1

Recursion applies decomposition by letting a function call itself on a smaller instance of the same problem. A correct recursive function has four parts:

  • Contract: one sentence stating exactly what f(input) returns.
  • Base case: the smallest input(s) answered directly, with no further call.
  • Reduction step: how the problem shrinks, such as n → n−1 or n → n//2.
  • Combination step: how the smaller answer builds the current answer.
python
def factorial(n): if n == 1: # base case return 1 return n * factorial(n - 1) # reduction and combination in one line

Here the reduction and combination share one line: n! = n × (n−1)!, with base case 1! = 1.

4.2Three safety questions

W4 · F.2

  • Is every smallest valid input handled? There may be more than one base case.
  • Does every call make progress towards a base case?
  • Can a call jump past the base case? If the base case is n == 1 but n = 0 is possible, subtracting 1 never lands on 1.

Infinite recursion means the base case is missing, unreachable, or placed after an unconditional recursive call. Python raises RecursionError after about 1000 nested calls.

4.3Tracing in two phases

W4 · F.3

A recursive call pauses the caller. Each unfinished call keeps its own parameters in a stack frame.

  • Phase A, calls go down: write each call, indent, and stop at a base case.
  • Phase B, values come up: start from the base value, substitute it into the paused caller, and continue upwards.
Calls going downValues returning up
factorial(4) waits for factorial(3)factorial(1) returns 1
factorial(3) waits for factorial(2)factorial(2) returns 2 × 1 = 2
factorial(2) waits for factorial(1)factorial(3) returns 3 × 2 = 6
factorial(1) is the base casefactorial(4) returns 4 × 6 = 24

Four calls, but only three multiplications: the base case does none. Recursion depth is the longest chain of simultaneously unfinished calls, and it sets the memory used.

4.4Branching recursion: Fibonacci

W4 · F.4

Fibonacci needs two base cases. Because each call makes two recursive calls, trace it as a call tree: in fibonacci(4), fibonacci(2) is computed twice.

python
def fibonacci(n): if n == 0: return 0 # two base cases: if n == 1: return 1 # fib(n-2) can land on either return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2) def fib_iter(n): # keeps only the last two values: O(n) a, b = 0, 1 for _ in range(n): a, b = b, a + b return a
  • The number of additions grows like 1.6ⁿ, with ratios settling near the golden ratio 1.618. Since 1.6ⁿ < 2ⁿ, both O(1.6ⁿ) and O(2ⁿ) are valid upper bounds.
  • The loop version runs n − 1 times: O(n).

Recursion is not automatically more efficient than iteration. It is a different way of expressing a solution.

4.5Halving is not automatically O(log n)

W4 · F.5

VersionCalls per levelResult
Reduce the exponent by 1One call, a chain16 multiplications for n = 16: O(n)
Halve the exponent, call twiceTwo callsT(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) = O(n); 47 multiplications for n = 16
Halve the exponent, save and reuse the half-powerOne callT(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n); 6 multiplications for n = 16

Halving gives O(log n) only when there is one recursive call per level. Writing the same call twice runs it twice, independently, unless you save the result.

4.6Recurrences

W4 · F.6

Let T(n) be the running time for input size n. Read one non-base invocation and work through these steps:

  • Name the input size and the base-case cost.
  • Count the recursive calls of one invocation, and write each smaller input size.
  • Compute the local work: what the current call does outside its recursive calls. Never count a recursive call as O(1); write it as T(smaller).
  • Write the recurrence, expand or draw the levels, sum the work, and only then simplify.
RecurrenceExpansionResult
T(n) = T(n−1) + cc + c + ⋯, n timesO(n)
T(n) = T(n/2) + clog₂ n calls of O(1)O(log n)
T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n)n + (n−1) + ⋯ + 1 = n(n+1)/2O(n²)
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n)n + n/2 + n/4 + ⋯ < 2nO(n), not O(n log n)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)Calls double while sizes halveO(n)

Always substitute the actual argument passed to an expensive helper at each level. A helper called on a fixed size k while n halves costs O(k log n).

4.7Common mistakes

W4 · F.7

SymptomCauseRepair
Crashes immediately, counting past 0No base caseTest the smallest input before recursing
Crashes though a base case is visibleBase case written after an unconditional recursive callMove the base-case test first
Every traceback line shows the same argumentReduction step forgottenWrite out the sequence of arguments by hand
Works for even n, not oddStep size jumps over the base caseUse an inequality or cover both parities
Answer is NoneA recursive value computed but never returnedEnd every branch with return
Answer always equals the base valueRecursive line omits its own part, such as n *Re-read the combination step
Small inputs misbehaveA second base case is missingList every smallest input the reduction can reach
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The four parts of every recursive function.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
ContractStates in one sentence what f(input) returns.A sentence, not code.
Base caseAnswers the smallest input directly, with no call.Makes the recursion stop.
Reduction stepShrinks the problem to a smaller instance of the same problem.Makes progress towards the base case.
Combination stepUses the smaller answer to build the current answer.Runs after the call returns.

The stack frame is not one of the four parts. It is where an unfinished call keeps its parameters while it waits.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4.1

Counting calls and operations

The problem

Trace factorial(4) and count calls and multiplications.

The trace
  • Calls going down: factorial(4), (3), (2), (1): four calls.
  • Values coming up: 1, then 2 × 1 = 2, 3 × 2 = 6, 4 × 6 = 24: three multiplications.
The lesson

The number of calls is not the number of operations; the base case does no multiplication.

WORKED EXAMPLE 4.2

Fibonacci additions

The problem

Count the additions made by recursive Fibonacci.

The trace
nAdditions
32

1088
The lesson

The count grows by a factor near 1.6 per step, which is exponential.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Cost of power1. power1(x, n) returns 1 when n == 0, otherwise x * power1(x, n-1). How many multiplications for x = 3, n = 16, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
16 multiplications, one per call down to n = 0. Complexity O(n).
2
Cost of power2. power2(x, n) returns 1 for n == 0; for even n it returns power2(x, n//2) * power2(x, n//2); for odd n it returns x * power2(x, n//2) * power2(x, n//2). How many multiplications for n = 16, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
Two recursive calls per level, so the instances double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 at n = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0. Multiplications: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16×2 + 32×0 = 47. An odd n costs 2 multiplications, an even n costs 1, and n = 0 costs 0. In general at most 2(n−1) + 2n multiplications, so O(n). Calling the halved problem once and reusing the result (power3) removes the doubling.
3
Merge sort just before the final merge. For [26, 34, 64, 83, 2, 5] and [52, 30, 98, 59, 67, 4, 64, 12, 79], give the array just before the final merge for the bottom-up and top-down versions.
Show answer
First array. Top-down (mid = len//2): the halves [26, 34, 64] and [83, 2, 5] are sorted first, giving [26, 34, 64, 2, 5, 83]. Bottom-up: runs of 4 and 2 remain, giving [26, 34, 64, 83, 2, 5]. Second array. Top-down: [30, 52, 59, 98, 4, 12, 64, 67, 79]. Bottom-up: [4, 12, 30, 52, 59, 64, 67, 98, 79], the last merge joining a run of 8 with a single element. The two versions reach different intermediate states, so say which version you are tracing.
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Pascal triangle recursion. Complete pt(n, k), where pt(n, k) = pt(n−1, k−1) + pt(n−1, k) and the first and last entries of each level are 1. Then trace pt(4, 2).
Show answer
if k == 1: return 1; if k == n + 1: return 1; return pt(n-1, k-1) + pt(n-1, k). pt(4, 2) = pt(3, 1) + pt(3, 2) = 1 + (pt(2, 1) + pt(2, 2)) = 1 + (1 + 2) = 4.
2
power3 with one recursive call. power3(x, n) returns 1 for n == 0; otherwise it computes temp = power3(x, n//2) and returns temp * temp for even n, or x * temp * temp for odd n. How many multiplications for x = 3 with n = 16 and n = 19, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
n = 16: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6. n = 19: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8. There are up to log₂ n + 1 instances with at most 2 multiplications each, so O(log n).
3
Recursive calls with a linear helper. sub_function is linear. What is the complexity of my_function(n) when it calls sub_function(n) then my_function(n//2); when it calls sub_function(k) with my_function(k, n//2); and when it calls sub_function(n) then my_function(n-1)?
Show answer
O(n): n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n. O(k log n): log n levels, each costing O(k). O(n²): n + (n−1) + … + 1.
4
Recursive maximum. Write a recursive max_array(a) without sorting.
Show answer
Slicing version: if len(a) == 1: return a[0], otherwise return max(a[0], max_array(a[1:])). A faster-copying version passes lower and upper: base cases when the range is empty or has one value, otherwise mid = (lower + upper) // 2 and return max(max_array(a, lower, mid), max_array(a, mid, upper)). Both are O(n) in the worst case, since every element must be examined.
5
Recursive palindrome. Write a recursive is_palindrome(s).
Show answer
Compare the first and last characters. Base cases: length 0 or 1 gives True; a mismatch gives False. Otherwise recurse on s[1:len(s)-1]. An index version keeps i and stops when i > len(s) − 1 − i. Worst case O(n).
6
Sign-alternating recurrence. f(n) returns 1 for n 0 or 1, otherwise −f(n−1) − f(n−2). Give f(1), f(5), f(6), f(330) and the worst-case complexity.
Show answer
f(1) = 1, f(5) = −2, f(6) = 1, f(330) = 1 (the values repeat with period 3: 1, 1, −2). Each call makes two calls on n−1 and n−2, so the worst case is exponential, about O(1.6ⁿ) or O(2ⁿ).
⚡ Quick examples
Reading a recurrence
PointOne call on n−1 with O(1) local work is a chain.
ExampleT(n) = T(n−1) + c gives O(n).
ExplanationThe c is added n times.
Saving a repeated call
PointStore a repeated recursive result instead of calling twice.
ExampleReuse the half-power when halving the exponent.
ExplanationOne call per level turns O(n) into O(log n).
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • A recursive function needs a contract, a base case, a reduction step and a combination step.
  • Check every smallest input, progress, and jumping past the base case.
  • Trace calls going down, then values coming up.
  • Branching recursion repeats work: Fibonacci is exponential, the loop is O(n).
  • Halving gives O(log n) only with one recursive call per level.
  • Write the recurrence from one invocation and expand it.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Why does Fibonacci need two base cases?tap to flip
fibonacci(n−2) can land on either 0 or 1.
Recursion depthtap to flip
The longest chain of simultaneously unfinished calls.
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n)tap to flip
O(n), because the sizes form a geometric sum below 2n.
Base case after a recursive calltap to flip
It is dead code, and the recursion never stops.
➡ Where next? Recursion keeps its pending work on a stack. Next, linear data structures make that stack explicit.

lessons.title: Linear Data Structures
lessons.goal: Use stacks, queues and priority queues, and cost them with an array.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Data structures decide which operations are cheap. A stack is what powers recursion.
🧠 Memory hook
Stack = LIFO, queue = FIFO. Only one end is accessible, and the cost depends on which end of the array it is.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Abstract data typesLinear structuresStack: push, pop, peekQueue: enqueue, dequeue, peekPriority queueLink back to recursion
⚡ At a glance — three linear structures
Stack: last in, first outQueue: first in, first outPriority queue: best priority out
5.1Abstract data types

W5 · G.1

An abstract data type (ADT) is defined by the operations it supports, not by how they are implemented. The representation is hidden from the client.

  • Localisation: changing the implementation does not break code that uses the ADT.
  • Flexibility: different implementations can be swapped in without the client noticing.

The List ADT supports create, insert, retrieve, remove and count at a position.

5.2Linear structures

W5 · G.2

In a linear data structure only one end is accessible.

StructureAccessible itemOrder
StackThe most recently added itemLIFO: last in, first out
QueueThe earliest added item still presentFIFO: first in, first out
5.3Stack: push, pop, peek

W5 · G.3

A stack exposes only its top. Push places an item on top, pop removes and returns the top, and peek inspects the top without removing it. Examples: backspace, browser back and the function call stack.

  • With a list whose top is index 0, push and pop cost O(n) because every item shifts.
  • With the top at the end of the list, append() and pop() cost O(1). The course Stack class uses the end.

Balanced braces: push each opening bracket. On a closing bracket, pop and check that the type matches. Fail if a closing bracket arrives too early, the type does not match, or openings remain at the end.

5.4Queue: enqueue, dequeue, peek

W5 · G.4

A queue removes at its head (oldest item) and inserts at its tail. Enqueue adds to the tail, dequeue removes and returns the head, and peek inspects the head. Examples: a checkout line and printer job spooling.

  • With a plain array whose head is index 0, enqueue is O(1) but dequeue is O(n), because the remaining items shift down.
  • Whichever end is removable, array operations at that end cost O(n).

Palindrome check: push and enqueue the same characters. The stack reverses order and the queue preserves it, so comparing pop against dequeue tests the palindrome. O(n) time and O(n) extra space.

5.5Priority queue

W5 · G.5

A priority queue is not first in, first out: dequeue and peek return the item with the best priority, whatever its arrival order. State the priority direction and a tie rule first.

Implementationenqueuepeekdequeue
Unsorted listO(1)O(n): scan for the bestO(n): scan, then delete
Sorted list, best at one endO(n): find and shiftO(1)O(1)
Binary search tree (§6.4)O(log n) average, O(n) worstO(1)O(log n) average, O(n) worst
Min-heap (§7.1)O(log n)O(1)O(log n)

No choice is best for every access pattern. If you enqueue rarely and dequeue often, a sorted list pays the ordering cost once per insertion and gets O(1) removals.

5.6Link back to recursion

W5 · G.6, G.8

A stack is what implements the call stack. A recursive function can be rewritten with an explicit stack that holds its pending parameters. Binary search pushes one branch per iteration, so its stack stays small, matching its O(log n) depth.

A queue from two stacks. Use IN for arriving items and OUT for leaving items. When OUT is empty, pop everything from IN and push it onto OUT, which reverses the order a second time. Popping OUT then returns the oldest item. One dequeue may cost O(n), but each item moves from IN to OUT only once, so the cost is amortised O(1).

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The three linear structures and their operations.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
StackExposes the top: push, pop, peek.Last in, first out.
QueueInserts at the tail, removes at the head: enqueue, dequeue, peek.First in, first out.
Priority queueSame operation names as a queue, but dequeue returns the best priority.Order depends on priority, not arrival.

A list is not one of the three: it allows access at any position. It is used to implement them.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5.1

Balanced braces with a stack

The problem

Decide whether { ( ) } is balanced.

The trace
SymbolActionStack (top at right)
{push{
(push{ (
)pop (, types match{
}pop {, types matchempty
The lesson

Balanced: every closing symbol matched the top, and the stack ended empty.

WORKED EXAMPLE 5.2

Queue from two stacks

The problem

Enqueue A, B, C, then dequeue.

The trace
  • IN is [A, B, C] with C on top; OUT is empty.
  • Dequeue finds OUT empty, so pop IN and push onto OUT: OUT becomes [C, B, A] with A on top.
  • Pop OUT: returns A, the oldest item.
The lesson

Reversing twice restores first-in, first-out order.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Browser back, forward and visit. Stacks U = [C, B, A] (C on top), current page D, R empty. Run: back, back, forward, visit(E), back. Record U, current page and R after each action.
Show answer
Start: U [C, B, A], current D, R []. back: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. back: U [A], current B, R [C, D]. forward: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. visit(E): U [C, B, A], current E, R [] (visit clears R). back: U [B, A], current C, R [E]. Forward is available because R is not empty and holds E.
2
Round-robin help desk. Queue [(A, 5), (B, 2), (C, 4)], head first. Each turn dequeues the head, processes min(2, remaining) minutes, then finishes the job or enqueues it at the tail. Give the completion order and number of turns.
Show answer
Turn 1: A 5 to 3, queue [B2, C4, A3]. Turn 2: B finishes. Turn 3: C 4 to 2, queue [A3, C2]. Turn 4: A 3 to 1, queue [C2, A1]. Turn 5: C finishes. Turn 6: A finishes. Completion order B, C, A in 6 turns. In general the turns equal Σ ⌈tᵢ/2⌉ and the number of queue operations is O(Σ tᵢ) for a fixed quantum.
3
Remove adjacent duplicates. Process ABBACA left to right with a stack: pop if the character equals the top, otherwise push.
Show answer
Stack after each character: [A], [A, B], [A] (second B cancels), [] (A cancels), [C], [C, A]. Final string, bottom to top: CA. Removing one pair can expose a new equal pair underneath, which the stack handles automatically. Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n).
4
Priority help desk. Smaller number is higher priority; ties go to the earlier arrival. Start with A(3), B(1), C(2). Perform: enqueue D(1); dequeue; enqueue E(2); dequeue; dequeue.
Show answer
After enqueue D(1): next order B, D, C, A. Dequeue returns B. Enqueue E(2): order D, C, E, A. Dequeue returns D. Dequeue returns C. The remaining queue is E(2), A(3), so the complete removal sequence is B, D, C, E, A.
5
Queue from two stacks. enqueue pushes onto IN. dequeue pops OUT, but if OUT is empty it first moves every IN value onto OUT. Trace: enqueue A, B, C, dequeue, enqueue D, dequeue, dequeue, enqueue E, dequeue.
Show answer
Enqueues leave IN [A, B, C]. First dequeue transfers, so OUT [C, B] after returning A. Enqueue D gives IN [D]. Dequeue returns B, then C (OUT empties). Enqueue E gives IN [D, E]. The last dequeue transfers and returns D, leaving OUT [E], so the next item is E. One dequeue is O(n) in the worst case (a transfer), but each element moves at most once, so the amortised cost is O(1) per operation. Auxiliary space O(n).
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Push and pop letters. A letter means push and * means pop. For the sequence A R D G * O * C A R E L D O * * C F U L * * C L O C * K * * *, give the letters popped from an initially empty stack, and the letters dequeued if a letter means enqueue and * means dequeue.
Show answer
Stack: GOODLUCKOL. Queue: ARDGOCAREL.
2
Weird queue. What queue does do_weird_stuff(6) return? For i in range(n): if i is odd, dequeue x and enqueue x + i; otherwise enqueue i.
Show answer
[4, 4, 7], with 4 at the head. Trace: [0], [1], [1, 2], [2, 4], [2, 4, 4], [4, 4, 7].
3
Which pop sequences are possible?. Numbers 1 to n are pushed in increasing order, with pops at any time. Give operations that print 1 3 5 4 2. Is there a sequence that cannot occur?
Show answer
Push 1, pop (1); push 2, push 3, pop (3); push 4, push 5, pop (5), pop (4), pop (2). Impossible example: 1 5 4 2 3. Once a value n₃ is popped, two smaller values that were pushed earlier cannot come out in increasing order, so 3, 1, 2 can never occur.
4
Invert, and delete, using the other structure. Invert a queue using a stack; invert a stack using a queue; delete one element from a stack using a queue while keeping the rest in order.
Show answer
Invert the queue: dequeue everything onto the stack, then pop everything back into the queue. Invert the stack: pop everything into the queue, then dequeue everything back onto the stack. Delete from the stack: pop each element into the queue unless it is the one to delete; push everything back (now reversed); pop into the queue again; push back (original order restored without the deleted element).
5
Non-recursive factorial. Convert the recursive factorial into a version that uses a stack.
Show answer
Push n; result = 1; while the stack is not empty, pop m, result *= m, and if m > 1 push m − 1. Return result.
⚡ Quick examples
Choosing the end of the array
PointPut the stack top at the end of the list.
Exampleappend() and pop() without an index.
ExplanationNo other item has to shift.
Priority queue trade-off
PointUnsorted list: cheap insert, costly removal.
ExampleSorted list: costly insert, cheap removal.
ExplanationPick by whether you insert or remove more often.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • An ADT is defined by its operations, not its implementation.
  • Stack is last in, first out; queue is first in, first out.
  • Put the stack top at the end of the array for O(1) push and pop.
  • An array queue has O(n) dequeue from the front.
  • A priority queue returns the best priority; a min-heap gives O(log n) for both ends.
  • A queue can be built from two stacks with amortised O(1) dequeue.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
LIFO or FIFO: stack?tap to flip
LIFO: last in, first out.
Cost of dequeue in a plain array queuetap to flip
O(n): the remaining items shift down.
Why does a two-stack queue reverse twice?tap to flip
Moving items from IN to OUT reverses the order, restoring FIFO.
Priority queue on a min-heaptap to flip
O(log n) enqueue and dequeue, O(1) peek.
➡ Where next? Linear structures expose one end. Trees add branching, and keep sorted order usable.

lessons.title: Trees
lessons.goal: Name tree parts and shapes, traverse binary trees, and see why BST shape sets its cost.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Trees add hierarchy, and a binary search tree keeps sorted order usable as data changes.
🧠 Memory hook
Shape is everything. Every BST operation costs at most the height, so balanced is O(log n) and skewed is O(n).
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Trees and their termsBinary tree shapesTraversalsBinary search treesBST efficiency: shape is everything
⚡ At a glance — traversals and the BST rule
Pre: parent firstIn: parent betweenPost: parent lastBST: left < node < right
6.1Trees and their terms

W6 · H.1

A tree is a root node plus zero or more subtrees, each rooted at one of its children. The recursive definition is why so many tree algorithms are recursive.

TermMeaning
RootThe topmost node
LeafA node with no children
Parent and childA direct relationship
Ancestor and descendantA relationship through a chain of parent–child links, direct or indirect
SiblingNodes that share the same parent
LevelThe root is level 1, its children level 2, and so on
HeightThe maximum level of any node; an empty tree has height 0
6.2Binary tree shapes

W6 · H.2

A binary tree gives each node at most two children, the left child and the right child.

ShapeDefinition
FullEvery node has exactly 0 or 2 children
CompleteEvery level except possibly the last is full, and the last level is packed as far left as possible
PerfectAll leaves are at the same depth and every internal node has exactly 2 children; with the root at level 1, height h gives 2ʰ − 1 nodes
Height-balancedAt every node, the left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1

Each name tests a different property. A full tree need not be complete: its deepest nodes can sit on the right with gaps on the left.

6.3Traversals

W6 · H.3

A traversal visits every node exactly once. The three orders differ only in when the parent is visited.

OrderVisit sequenceMemory aid
PreorderParent, left subtree, right subtreeParent first
InorderLeft subtree, parent, right subtreeParent in the middle
PostorderLeft subtree, right subtree, parentParent last

Each is O(n): every node is visited once with O(1) work. On a BST, inorder visits keys in ascending order.

6.4Binary search trees

W6 · H.4

Searching an unordered tree costs O(n), like linear search. A binary search tree (BST) imposes an order: for every node, every value in its left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger.

  • Search: compare, then go left or right.
  • Insert: a new key goes exactly where searching for it would have failed.

Removing a node: three cases

  • Leaf: detach it.
  • One child: the parent adopts that child.
  • Two children: replace it with the successor (the left-most node of the right subtree) or the predecessor (the right-most node of the left subtree). Both give valid BSTs with different shapes.

Deleting 8 from the tree above: the successor is 10 (go right to 12, then left as far as possible); the predecessor is 6 (go left to 4, then right as far as possible).

6.5BST efficiency: shape is everything

W6 · H.5

The maximum number of comparisons for search, insert or remove equals the height, because each comparison descends one level.

  • A balanced tree of n nodes has height about ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, so operations are O(log n).
  • A completely skewed tree (each node has one child, like a linked list) has height n, so operations are O(n).
  • For a non-empty BST with root at level 1, ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ ≤ h ≤ n.

Insertion order decides the shape. Inserting already sorted data one key at a time gives the worst shape. Inserting the middle element first, then recursively the middles of each half, gives a balanced tree.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The four binary tree shapes. Each tests a different property.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
FullEvery node has 0 or 2 children.Never exactly one child.
CompleteLevels fill top to bottom, the last level left to right.Concerns position, not child counts.
PerfectAll leaves at one depth, every internal node has 2 children.Both full and complete, plus equal depth.
Height-balancedSubtree heights differ by at most 1 at every node.Concerns height, not fullness.

Balanced is not the same as complete or perfect: a height-balanced tree can have gaps at the last level.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 6.1

Insertion order and shape

The problem

Build a BST from the keys 2, 10, 4, 7, 19, 5, 8, 11, 3, 15 by inserting them left to right.

The trace
  • Preorder: 2, 10, 4, 3, 7, 5, 8, 19, 11, 15.
  • Postorder: 3, 5, 8, 7, 4, 15, 11, 19, 10, 2.
  • Inserting the same keys in strictly increasing order makes every node a right child, so the tree becomes a chain of height 10.
The lesson

The same keys give different shapes. Sorted insertion is the worst case.

📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Tree terminology. For the tree in the tutorial sheet, name the root, the leaf nodes, and the parent, children, descendants, ancestor and sibling of node 14.
Show answer
Root 29. Leaves 2, 27 and 71. Parent of 14 is 29. Children of 14 are 2 and 24. Descendants of 14 are 2, 24 and 27. Ancestor of 14 is 29. Sibling of 14 is 50.
2
Cars BST: insertion order against alphabetical order. Insert Lexus, Mercedes, BMW, Audi, Lamborghini, Chevrolet, Porsche, Maserati, Lotus into a BST in that order. Count comparisons to find Audi, Lamborghini, Maserati and Porsche. Repeat when inserting in alphabetical order.
Show answer
Listed order: Audi 3, Lamborghini 3, Maserati 3, Porsche 3 comparisons. Alphabetical order creates a chain (every node is the right child of the previous one): Audi 1, Lamborghini 4, Maserati 7, Porsche 9 comparisons.
3
Badminton tournament. There are 14 participants; each game eliminates one player and an odd player out is promoted automatically. How many games are needed, and what is the complexity in n?
Show answer
Round 1: 7 games; round 2: 3; round 3: 2; round 4: 1. Total 13 games. In general n − 1 games, so O(n) (13 people need 12 games, 12 people need 11).
4
TreeSort. Insert each element into a BST, then traverse to print in sorted order. Which traversal, and what is the worst-case complexity?
Show answer
In-order traversal. Inserting n elements costs O(n²) in the worst case (a chain) and the traversal costs O(n), so the overall worst case is O(n²).
5
Could this array be a BST postorder?. Design an algorithm that returns True if an array of distinct numbers could be the postorder traversal of some BST, and give its worst-case complexity.
Show answer
Brute force: try every permutation as an insertion order and compare postorders, O(n! · n²). Better: the last element is the root. Find a split point so everything before it is smaller than the root and everything after is larger, then check both parts recursively; no split point means False. Worst case O(n²). Another way: reverse the array, insert it into a BST (O(n²)), take the postorder (O(n)), and compare with the input.
6
BST from an array and traversals. Build the BST by inserting A = [2, 10, 4, 7, 19, 5, 8, 11, 3, 15] left to right. Give the preorder and postorder traversals, then reorder A into B so that the BST has the worst-case chain shape.
Show answer
Preorder 2, 10, 4, 3, 7, 5, 8, 19, 11, 15. Postorder 3, 5, 8, 7, 4, 15, 11, 19, 10, 2. For the zig-zag chain shape the root must be the smallest element and the second level the largest, and so on, which gives B = [2, 19, 3, 15, 4, 11, 5, 10, 7, 8].
⚡ Quick examples
Reading a traversal
PointCheck where the parent falls among its subtrees.
ExamplePreorder of the root-8 tree starts with 8; inorder gives 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.
ExplanationThe word "in" marks the parent in the middle.
Tree height
PointHeight is the maximum level, with the root at level 1.
ExampleA chain of 10 nodes has height 10.
ExplanationSearch cost is bounded by the height.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • A tree is a root plus subtrees; the root is level 1 and height is the maximum level.
  • Full, complete, perfect and height-balanced test different properties.
  • Preorder is parent first, inorder parent in the middle, postorder parent last; each is O(n).
  • A BST has smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right.
  • Removing a node has three cases; two children use the successor or predecessor.
  • BST operations cost the height: O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Which traversal sorts a BST?tap to flip
Inorder.
Two-children deletiontap to flip
Replace with the successor (left-most of the right subtree) or the predecessor.
Worst-case BST shapetap to flip
A chain, built by inserting sorted data.
Height bounds of a BST with n nodestap to flip
⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ ≤ h ≤ n.
➡ Where next? A BST can still skew. Next, heaps keep a tree complete so its height stays O(log n).

lessons.title: Heaps
lessons.goal: Build and repair a min-heap, and use it for priority queues and sorting.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
A heap keeps a tree complete, so a priority queue costs O(log n) at both ends.
🧠 Memory hook
Two rules, one path. Complete shape plus parent ≤ children. Every repair follows a single root-to-leaf path.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
What a heap isStoring a heap in an arrayInsert: append, then up-heapremoveMin: save the root, then down-heapCost of a heap priority queueBuildHeap in O(n)Sorting with a priority queue
⚡ At a glance — heap operations
insert: append, up-heapremoveMin: last to root, down-heapbuildHeap: O(n)heap sort: O(n log n)
7.1What a heap is

W7a · J.1–J.2

A min-heap obeys two separate rules:

  • Shape rule: the tree is complete, so its height is always ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 nodes.
  • Heap-order rule: every parent is ≤ both of its children.

No path ever decreases going down, so the minimum is at the root. [2, 5, 4, 9, 8, 7] is a valid min-heap. [2, 5, 4, 1] is not: the key 1 is the child of 5.

Binary search treeMin-heap
Ordering ruleLeft subtree < node < right subtreeParent ≤ both children
Shape ruleNone; can become a chainMust be complete
HeightO(log n) to O(n)Always ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1
Fast atSearching for any keyFinding and removing the minimum
Search for an arbitrary keyO(height)O(n): order does not say which subtree to try
Inorder traversalSortedNot sorted in general
7.2Storing a heap in an array

W7a · J.3

A complete tree needs no pointers. Store it level by level, with 0-based indices:

RelationshipIndex
Root0
Left child of j2j + 1
Right child of j2j + 2
Parent of j (not the root)⌊(j − 1)/2⌋
Last parent⌊n/2⌋ − 1

A child index must be less than n to exist. In a 10-entry heap, index 4 has a left child at 9, but 10 is not a valid index.

7.3Insert: append, then up-heap

W7a · J.4

  • Append the key at index n. This is the only placement that keeps the tree complete.
  • The new leaf can only break the rule with its parent.
  • Up-heap: swap upward while the key is smaller than its parent. Stop at the root, or when parent ≤ child.

One swap per level at most, so O(log n). The best case is O(1).

7.4removeMin: save the root, then down-heap

W7a · J.5

  • Save the root: it is the answer.
  • Move the last entry into the root and shorten the array. This is the only removal that keeps the tree complete.
  • Down-heap: compare with both children, swap with the smaller one if it is smaller, and repeat until neither child is smaller.

Swapping with the smaller child guarantees the new parent is ≤ both children. Swapping with the larger one would make it a parent of a smaller key. The cost is one root-to-leaf path: O(log n).

7.5Cost of a heap priority queue

W7a · J.6

MethodHeap-based priority queue
size, isEmpty, minO(1)
insertO(log n)
removeMinO(log n)

Inserting n keys one at a time costs Σ O(log i), which is O(n log n) in the worst case.

7.6BuildHeap in O(n)

W7a · J.8

  • Treat the array as a complete tree.
  • Skip the leaves: they are already one-node heaps.
  • From the last parent, index ⌊n/2⌋ − 1, back to the root, run down-heap on each node.

Going bottom-up works because, when node j is repaired, both child subtrees are already valid heaps, which is the precondition of down-heap.

Why O(n) and not O(n log n): most nodes sit near the leaves and fall only a short way. In a full tree of 15 nodes, 1 node can fall 3 levels, 2 nodes 2 levels, 4 nodes 1 level and 8 leaves 0 levels: at most 1·3 + 2·2 + 4·1 + 8·0 = 11 swaps. The bound for 7 nodes is 4 and for 31 nodes is 26.

7.7Sorting with a priority queue

W7a · J.9

Put all items into a priority queue (phase 1), then repeatedly remove the minimum (phase 2). The queue's implementation decides the algorithm.

Priority queuePhase 1Phase 2AlgorithmWorst case
Unsorted listn × O(1)n × O(n) scanSelection sortO(n²)
Sorted listn × O(n)n × O(1)Insertion sortO(n²)
Heapn × O(log n)n × O(log n)Heap sortO(n log n)
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
Three sorting algorithms from one priority-queue scheme.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Selection sortUnsorted-list queue: append, then scan for the minimum each time.Phase 1 is cheap.
Insertion sortSorted-list queue: insert in place, then take from the front.Phase 2 is cheap.
Heap sortHeap queue: O(log n) insert and O(log n) removal.Both phases cost O(log n) per item.

Merge sort is not part of this set: it does not use a priority queue.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 7.1

The problem

The lesson

The new key rises one level per swap, at most the height.

WORKED EXAMPLE 7.2

Remove the minimum from [3, 7, 4, 15, 10, 12, 9].

The trace

Save rootReturn 3
Move last (9) to root[9, 7, 4, 15, 10, 12]Children 7 and 4; the smaller is 4
Swap 9 and 4[4, 7, 9, 15, 10, 12]Only child of 9 is 12, and 9 ≤ 12, so stop
The lesson

Down-heap picks the smaller child so the new parent stays ≤ both children.

WORKED EXAMPLE 7.3

The trace
Parent indexSwapsArray after

📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Priority queue operations. Run the sequence: insert(5, A), insert(4, B), insert(7, F), insert(1, D), removeMin, insert(3, J), insert(6, L), removeMin, removeMin, insert(8, G), removeMin, insert(2, H), removeMin, removeMin. What does each removeMin return?
Show answer
In order: (1, D), (3, J), (4, B), (5, A), (2, H), (6, L).
2
Array indices of a complete tree of 15 nodes. A heap stores 15 entries in an array at indices 0 to 14. Give the index sequence for preorder, inorder and postorder traversals.
Show answer
Preorder 0, 1, 3, 7, 8, 4, 9, 10, 2, 5, 11, 12, 6, 13, 14. Inorder 7, 3, 8, 1, 9, 4, 10, 0, 11, 5, 12, 2, 13, 6, 14. Postorder 7, 8, 3, 9, 10, 4, 1, 11, 12, 5, 13, 14, 6, 2, 0.
3
k smallest numbers with a heap. Describe a heap-based algorithm to find the k smallest numbers in an unordered collection of N numbers and give its complexity.
Show answer
Use buildHeap on all N numbers (O(N)), then call removeMin k times (O(k log N)), total O(N + k log N). In the worst case k = N this is O(N log N). Building by repeated insertion instead costs O(N log N + k log N).
4

Show answer
In the tutorial example, repeated insertion needed 9 swaps and gave [27, 39, 65, 43, 44, 88, 82, 83, 45, 79], while bottom-up buildHeap needed 7 swaps and gave [27, 39, 65, 43, 44, 82, 88, 45, 83, 79]. Bottom-up construction is O(n) while repeated insertion is O(n log n).

  • Store it in an array: children 2j+1 and 2j+2, parent ⌊(j−1)/2⌋.
  • Insert appends then up-heaps; O(log n).
  • removeMin moves the last entry to the root, then down-heaps with the smaller child; O(log n).
  • BuildHeap runs down-heap from the last parent back to the root in O(n).
  • A priority queue gives selection sort (unsorted), insertion sort (sorted) or heap sort (heap, O(n log n)).
