lessons.title: Hash Maps
lessons.goal: Compute where a key lives, handle collisions, and know the cost of a hash table.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
A hash map computes the row from the key, giving expected O(1) lookup where a list needs O(n).
🧠 Memory hook
Hash, then resolve. Hash the key to a row, then decide what happens when two keys want the same row.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
The problem with a listHash functions and tablesCollisions are inevitableSeparate chainingLinear probingComparing the strategies, and costs
⚡ At a glance — from key to row
key→hash function→row 0 … N−1→resolve collisions
8.1The problem with a list

W7b · K.1

A key/value collection in an unsorted list costs O(n) for get, put and remove, because each must first search for the key. Keys are unique, so even put must look for an existing key first.

8.2Hash functions and tables

W7b · K.2

A hash function turns a key into a row number. It is built in two stages:

  • Turn the key into an integer. For a word, read it as a base-26 number, with letters as digits 0–25.
  • Take the remainder by the table size N: row = integer % N, always in 0 … N−1.

Reading only the first letter works for a table of exactly 26 rows and piles together every word with the same first letter. The remainder step avoids a table of trillions of rows.

A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across the table and is deterministic: the same key always gives the same row.

8.3Collisions are inevitable

W7b · K.3

A collision occurs when two different keys hash to the same row. Collisions are common even with a good hash function. With a perfectly random hash and 100 words:

Table size NProbability of at least one collision
1,00099.29%
10,00039.04%
100,0004.83%
1,000,0000.49%

A bigger table helps, but less than intuition suggests.

8.4Separate chaining

W7b · K.4

Each row holds a bucket, a list of all entries that hash there. With n entries and N rows, the load factor is λ = n/N, the average bucket length.

  • Buckets can grow without limit, so λ can exceed 1.
  • A lookup scans one bucket only. A large λ makes buckets longer and lookups slower.
  • Deletion removes the entry from its bucket.
8.5Linear probing

W7b · K.5

Linear probing stores every entry in the main array, at most one per row.

  • Insert: if A[h(k)] is occupied, try A[(h(k) + i) % N] for i = 1, 2, …. The % N wraps from the last row to row 0.
  • Lookup: follow the same probe sequence. Stop when you find the key or reach a never-used empty row.
  • Delete: leave a deletion marker (tombstone). Emptying the row would create a fake hole that stops later lookups too early.
A lookup sees…Action
The matching keyReturn its value
A different keyContinue to the next row
A deletion markerContinue
A never-used empty rowStop: the key is absent
8.6Comparing the strategies, and costs

W7b · K.5–K.7

Separate chainingLinear probing
Where colliding keys goSame row's bucketThe next free row(s) in the main array
Entries per rowAny numberAt most one
Can λ exceed 1?YesNo: the table can fill up
DeletionRemove from the bucketLeave a marker
Worst-case lookupO(n): one long bucketO(N): scan the table
Typical weaknessLong buckets when N is smallClustering of occupied rows
MethodUnsorted listHash table, expectedHash table, worst
get, put, removeO(n)O(1)O(n)
size, isEmptyO(1)O(1)O(1)
entrySet, keySet, valuesO(n)O(n)O(n)

Do not use a hash table when you need the data in order. Hashing deliberately scatters keys, so use a sorted structure or a BST instead.

A Python dict is a hash table, and a set is a hash table of keys only. Membership tests are expected O(1), so a single pass that checks each needed partner value in a set runs in O(n) expected time.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The two collision strategies.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Separate chainingEach row holds a bucket list of its entries.Colliding keys share one row; λ can exceed 1.
Linear probingColliding keys move to the next free row, wrapping with % N.One entry per row; needs deletion markers.

Separate chaining is not a form of open addressing. Linear probing is: every entry lives in the main array.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 8.1

Chaining and probing on the same keys

The problem

Table size N = 7, h(k) = k mod 7. Insert 10, 17, 24 and 8.

The trace
KeyHome rowChainingLinear probing: rows tested, placed at
103Row 3: [10]3, placed at 3
173Row 3: [10, 17]3, 4, placed at 4
243Row 3: [10, 17, 24]3, 4, 5, placed at 5
81Row 1: [8]1, placed at 1

With chaining, λ = 4/7, and looking up 24 scans only row 3's bucket.

The lesson

Both strategies agree on home rows; they differ in where the colliding keys end up.

WORKED EXAMPLE 8.2

Why deletion needs a marker

The problem

Rows 3, 4, 5 hold 10, 17, 24 under linear probing. Delete 17, then look up 24.

The trace
Row 4 after deletionLookup of 24Correct?
Ordinary empty rowRow 3, then row 4 is empty, so stop and report "not found"No: 24 is still at row 5
Deletion markerRow 3, row 4 (marker, continue), row 5: foundYes
The lesson

A deletion marker keeps the probe chain unbroken.

📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
A legal but poor hash code. Is a hash_code() that gives every key the same value legal? Describe the effect.
Show answer
It is legal, but inappropriate: all keys land in the same cell, so the table degenerates into an unsorted table map and a search takes O(n) in the worst case.
2
Two numbers that sum to x. Design an algorithm that takes O(n) on average to decide whether an array of n numbers has two elements whose sum is a given x. Consider a hash map.
Show answer
Store the elements in a hash map. For each element a, check whether x − a is already in the map (an O(1) average lookup). Return True when found; otherwise add a and continue. One pass, O(n) on average.
⚡ Quick examples
Computing a row
PointTake the integer form of the key modulo N.
Exampleh(k) = k mod 7 sends 17 to row 3.
ExplanationThe remainder is always in 0 … 6.
Load factor
Pointλ = n/N.
Example4 entries in 7 rows gives λ = 4/7.
ExplanationIt is the average bucket length under chaining.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • A hash function has two stages: integer, then remainder by N.
  • Good hash functions are uniform and deterministic.
  • Collisions are inevitable and common.
  • Chaining keeps buckets; λ = n/N can exceed 1.
  • Linear probing uses the next free row with wrap-around, and needs deletion markers.
  • Expected O(1) for get, put and remove; worst case O(n); no sorted order.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Two properties of a good hash functiontap to flip
Uniform distribution and determinism.
Load factortap to flip
n/N: entries per row.
Why a deletion marker?tap to flip
An empty row would stop later lookups too early.
Worst-case get in a hash tabletap to flip
O(n).
➡ Where next? Hash maps find a key fast. Next, graphs connect many items together.

lessons.title: Graphs: Traversal and Topological Sort
lessons.goal: Represent graphs, traverse them with BFS and DFS, and order a DAG topologically.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Graphs model networks, and BFS and DFS put the queue and stack of earlier chapters to work.
🧠 Memory hook
Queue = nearest first, stack = deepest first. Both run in O(V + E) with lists.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Graph terminologyRepresenting a graphBreadth-first searchDepth-first searchRunning timeDAGs and topological sort
⚡ At a glance — graph toolkit
BFS: queue, fewest edgesDFS: stack, deep firstLists: O(V + E)Matrix: O(V²)Topological sort: DFS plus stack
9.1Graph terminology

W9 · L.1–L.2

A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. Networks of every kind fit: transport, communication, the web, dependencies and social links.

TermMeaning
Directed edge u → vTravel from u to v only; it does not imply v → u
Undirected edge u — vUsable both ways: two opposite directed edges
Neighbours of uThe targets in u's adjacency list
In-degree and out-degreeNumber of incoming and outgoing edges; count edges, not weights
PathVertices with consecutive pairs joined by an edge; length = number of edges = vertices − 1
Simple pathA path with no repeated vertex
CycleA path that starts and ends at the same vertex
DAGA directed graph with no cycles
Weighted graphEach edge carries a number such as distance, time or cost
  • Directed graph: Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|. In the example, both sums are 10.
  • Maximum edges in a simple graph on n vertices: directed n(n−1), undirected n(n−1)/2, and DAG n(n−1)/2.
  • A→B→D→F is a simple path of length 3. A→B→C→A is a cycle. A→B→D→B→E is a path but not simple.
9.2Representing a graph

W9 · L.3

Adjacency listAdjacency matrix
StructureOne row per vertex listing out-neighboursn × n grid; row = from, column = to
SpaceO(V + E)O(V²)
Edge u → v present?Scan the list: O(out-degree)O(1): read one cell
List neighbours of uO(out-degree)O(V): read the whole row
Undirected edgeAppears in both listsMatrix is symmetric
WeightedStore (neighbour, weight)Store the weight; use ∞ for no edge, since 0 can be a real weight
9.3Breadth-first search

W9 · L.4

BFS visits everything one edge away, then two edges away, and so on. A FIFO queue delivers that order. Mark a vertex when it is enqueued, so a shared neighbour is queued only once.

In an unweighted graph, the first time BFS discovers a vertex it has found a path with the fewest edges. It does not minimise total weight when weights differ.

9.4Depth-first search

W9 · L.5–L.6

DFS follows one path as far as it goes and backs up only when stuck. The recursion uses the call stack; an explicit stack can replace it.

  • Week 9 convention: mark on pop, and push neighbours in reverse list order, so the first-listed neighbour is explored first, matching the recursive order.
  • Week 10 questions may say "push in alphabetical order", which explores the last neighbour first. Follow the wording exactly.
  • The explicit stack holds alternatives waiting to be tried, not a chain of paused calls. Test "visited?" after every pop.
BFSDFS
ContainerQueue (FIFO)Stack (LIFO), explicit or the call stack
ExploresNearest vertices first, layer by layerOne path as deep as possible, then backtracks
Fewest-edge paths?Yes, if unweightedNo
Natural usesHop count, degrees of separationPath following, cycle exploration, topological sort
9.5Running time

W9 · L.7

  • Adjacency list: each vertex is visited once and each adjacency entry checked once, so O(V + E). Do not multiply V × E.
  • Adjacency matrix: reading a whole row costs V for each of V vertices, so O(V²).

In the running example, lists need 6 visits and 10 neighbour checks, while the matrix reads 36 cells of which only 10 hold a 1. A sparse graph favours lists.

9.6DAGs and topological sort

W9 · L.8

An edge A → B means B depends on A, so A must come first. A cycle is a contradiction. A topological ordering lists every vertex once so that for every edge u → v, u comes before v.

  • Every DAG has at least one ordering, and many have several. A graph with a cycle has none.
  • The first vertex must have in-degree 0.
  • DFS method: when a vertex's recursive call finishes, everything that must come after it has already finished. Push each vertex onto a stack as its call completes; popping gives the order.

The course DAG A:[B,C], B:[C,D,E], C:[D], D:[F], E:[D], F:[] has two valid orderings: A, B, E, C, D, F and A, B, C, E, D, F. The adjacency-list order decides which one DFS returns.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The graph search and ordering procedures.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Breadth-first search (BFS)Visits layer by layer using a queue.Queue, nearest first.
Depth-first search (DFS)Follows one path deep, then backtracks, using a stack.Stack, deepest first.
Topological sortOrders the vertices of a DAG so every edge points forward.DFS plus a stack of finished vertices.

Topological sort applies only to a DAG. Breadth-first search is not the same as a topological order.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 9.1

BFS on the running example

The problem

Run BFS from A on the graph above. Write the queue with head on the left.

The trace
StepDequeuedNewly visitedQueue after
0–A[A]
1AB, C[B, C]
2BD, E[C, D, E]
3C–[D, E]
4DF[E, F]
5E–[F]
6F–[ ]

Visit order: A, B, C, D, E, F. Layers: {A}, {B, C}, {D, E}, {F}.

The lesson

Each layer is one edge farther from the start.

WORKED EXAMPLE 9.2

DFS on the running example

The problem

Run recursive DFS from A, taking neighbours in list order.

The trace
  • Enter A, then B, then C. C's neighbours A and D: A is visited, so enter D.
  • D's neighbours B and F: B is visited, so enter F. F has no neighbours, so return.
  • Back at B, D is visited, so enter E. Order: A, B, C, D, F, E.
The lesson

DFS and BFS visit the same vertices in different orders.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Represent a directed graph. Vertices A to F; edges in order A→B, A→C, B→D, C→B, C→E, D→E, E→C; F is isolated. Give the adjacency list, the degree table and the number of edges.
Show answer
Adjacency list: A [B, C], B [D], C [B, E], D [E], E [C], F []. In-degrees A0 B2 C2 D1 E2 F0 and out-degrees A2 B1 C2 D1 E1 F0. Both sums are 7, so there are 7 directed edges. The matrix has row = source and column = target, and F still gets a row and column of zeros.
2
BFS and a fewest-edge route. Run BFS from A on that graph (mark on enqueue). Give the visit sequence, the unreached vertices, and a fewest-edge route from A to E.
Show answer
Queue: [A], then [B, C], [C, D], [D] (C adds nothing new), [E], []. Visit sequence A, B, C, D, E. F is unreached because no edge leads into it. The fewest-edge route is A → C → E (2 edges), since BFS explores layer by layer and E first appears from C.
3
Recursive DFS against stack DFS. Trace both DFS versions on the same graph from A. The stack version pushes neighbours in reverse list order and marks on pop.
Show answer
Recursive: A, B, D, E, C. Explicit stack: 6 pops, 5 new visits, visit sequence A, B, D, E, C. The extra pop is a duplicate C that was already visited, which is skipped (pending duplicates are allowed). The two sequences agree here, and F is unreached.
4
Topological order of a showcase plan. Adjacency lists A [C, D], B [D], C [E], D [E], E [], F []; outer loop order A to F; DFS-based method with a finish stack.
Show answer
Finish-stack pushes in order: E, C, D, A, B, F. Popping gives the order F, B, A, D, C, E. Every edge points forward. Of the proposed orders, A, B, C, D, E, F is valid, but A, C, D, B, E, F is not, because B must come before D (edge B → D). Adding E → A creates the cycle A → C → E → A, so no topological order exists.
5
Hops against total weight. Edges S→A 2, S→B 6, S→T 9, A→B 1, A→T 8, B→T 2. Compare the four S-to-T routes by edge count and total weight.
Show answer
S→T has 1 edge and weight 9. S→A→T has 2 edges and weight 10. S→B→T has 2 edges and weight 8. S→A→B→T has 3 edges and weight 5. The fewest-edge route is S→T but the minimum-weight route is S→A→B→T, result (5, [S, A, B, T]). BFS guarantees the fewest edges, not the lowest weight.
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Degrees, BFS and DFS of a 10-vertex graph. A to J with edges A→B, I; B→D, H; C→D; D→H; E→F, G; F→A; G→J; H→E; I→B, J; J→A. Give the highest in-degree and out-degree vertices and the BFS and DFS sequences from A.
Show answer
Highest in-degree (2): A, B, D, H, J. Highest out-degree (2): A, B, E, I. BFS from A: A B I D H J E F G. DFS from A: A B D H E F G J I.
2
Course prerequisites as a graph. IS200, PMSB and DM have no prerequisites; OOAD needs IS200; SE needs OOAD; EI needs OOAD, DM and PMSB; AA needs IS200 and EI; EWS needs SE and EI. Run DFS from IS200 and give one valid study order.
Show answer
Edges point from prerequisite to course. DFS from IS200 (vertex order IS200, DM, OOAD, SE, EI, AA, EWS, PMSB): IS200 → OOAD → SE → EWS → EI → AA. PMSB and DM are not reached from IS200. One valid order over 8 terms: IS200, OOAD, SE, PMSB, DM, EI, EWS, AA.
3
Make a graph acyclic. Adjacency list A [B, E, F], B [C, D, F], C [D], D [F], E [D, F], F [C]. Which node is visited right after F in DFS from A? Invert one edge to get a DAG and give a topological order.
Show answer
DFS: A, B, C, D, F, then E, so E follows F. Inverting the edge F → C to C → F removes the cycle C → D → F → C, and a topological order is A, E, B, C, D, F.
⚡ Quick examples
Reading a matrix
PointRow is the source, column is the target.
ExampleRow B, column D holds 1 for the edge B→D.
ExplanationReading column to row swaps incoming and outgoing edges.
Representation first
PointState the representation before quoting a time.
ExampleO(V + E) for lists, O(V²) for a matrix.
ExplanationA matrix scan counts absent edges too.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • A path's length is its number of edges; Σ in = Σ out = |E|.
  • Lists cost O(V + E) space and traversal; matrices cost O(V²).
  • BFS uses a queue, marks on enqueue, and finds fewest-edge paths in unweighted graphs.
  • DFS goes deep; Week 9 stack DFS pushes neighbours in reverse list order.
  • A topological ordering exists exactly for a DAG, and is not unique.
  • Topological sort: DFS, push each vertex when its call finishes, then pop.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then click the card.
Length of a pathtap to flip
The number of edges, one less than the number of vertices.
Why mark BFS vertices on enqueue?tap to flip
A shared neighbour would otherwise be queued twice.
Matrix traversal costtap to flip
O(V²).
Which graphs have a topological order?tap to flip
Exactly the DAGs.
➡ Where next? Traversals ignore weights. Next, search costs along weighted edges.

lessons.title: Graph Search and Shortest Paths
lessons.goal: Treat problems as state-space search, and find the cheapest path with uniform cost search.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Hop count is not cost. Uniform cost search finds the cheapest path when edges carry weights.
🧠 Memory hook
Cheapest first. Expand the vertex with the least total cost so far, using a priority queue.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Search as graph traversalHops are not costUniform cost searchBFS, DFS and UCS compared
⚡ At a glance — the frontier decides the strategy
BFS: queue→DFS: stack→UCS: priority queue
10.1Search as graph traversal

W10 · M.1

Many problems become graph search once you define states. A state describes a complete situation, an edge is a legal move between states, and the goal is a sequence of actions that leads to a goal state.

  • Farmer's problem: ferry a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river. A state records who is on the starting bank.
  • Invalid states: any bank with the wolf and goat, or the goat and cabbage, without the farmer.
  • Repeated states: a state already seen. Exploring it again only loops.
10.2Hops are not cost

W10 · M.2, W9 · L.9

In a weighted graph, the route with the fewest edges is not always the cheapest. Sum the weights separately. BFS minimises edges and ignores weights.

10.3Uniform cost search

W10 · M.3

Uniform cost search (UCS) always expands the vertex with the least total cost from the start so far. The candidates sit in a priority queue whose priority is that path cost, smaller meaning higher priority.

  • Update rule: a vertex still in the queue may later be reached more cheaply. Keep only the cheaper entry, with its new from-vertex.
  • Stop when the target is dequeued, not when it is first enqueued.
  • With non-negative weights, any other path to the dequeued vertex must pass through a frontier vertex that already costs at least as much.

UCS is treated as Dijkstra's algorithm run until every vertex is finalised, instead of stopping at one target. To recover the path, follow the previous-vertex links back from the target.

10.4BFS, DFS and UCS compared

W10 · M.3

BFSDFSUCS

Show answer
Step 1: dequeue A(0), enqueue B(2, A). Step 2: dequeue B(2), enqueue C(5, B) and E(4, B). Step 3: dequeue E(4), enqueue F(9, E). Step 4: dequeue C(5); D(6, C) is enqueued and F via C costs 9, which is not strictly lower, so F is unchanged. Step 5: dequeue D(6); G(7, D) is enqueued and F via D costs 9, unchanged. Step 6: dequeue G(7), the target, and stop. Following previous links gives the path A → B → C → D → G with total cost 7.

  • UCS expands the least total cost so far using a priority queue.

  • UCS stops when the target is dequeued and needs non-negative weights.
  • BFS uses a queue, DFS a stack, UCS a priority queue.

lessons.title: Heuristics: TSP, Greedy and Local Search
lessons.goal: Trade guaranteed optimality for speed with greedy construction and local search.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
For problems like the travelling salesman, exact search is hopeless. Heuristics give good answers fast.
🧠 Memory hook
Pick two of three: general, optimal, fast. Heuristics keep general and fast, and give up optimal.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
The travelling salesman problemOptimisation and the "pick two" trade-offBaselines: exhaustive and random searchGreedy construction: nearest neighbourGreedy construction: cheapest-side insertionLocal search and 2-optGreedy beyond TSP, and when it fails
⚡ At a glance — strategies for TSP
Exhaustive: optimal, O(n!)Random search: O(kn)Nearest neighbour: O(n²)Cheapest-side insertion: O(n³)2-opt: O(n²) per iteration
11.1The travelling salesman problem

W11 · N.1–N.2

In the travelling salesman problem (TSP) you visit every city once and return to the start, minimising the total distance.

A tour is a cycle, so its starting city does not matter. With n cities there are n! orderings, each tour appears n times, giving (n−1)!. With symmetric distances a tour and its reverse are equal, giving (n−1)!/2.

Cities n5678910
Tours (n−1)!/212603602,52020,160181,440
VariantNumber of tours
Round trip, symmetric distances(n−1)!/2
Round trip, asymmetric distances(n−1)!: a reversal is a different tour
Open path, symmetricn!/2
Open path, asymmetricn!
11.2Optimisation and the "pick two" trade-off

W11 · N.3

An optimisation problem has a value that indicates how good a solution is. Among general, optimal and fast, you can pick two:

PickYou getExample
General and optimalVery slowBrute force, exhaustive search
Fast and optimalOnly special casesA TSP whose cities lie on a line
Fast and generalNot guaranteed optimal, often good enoughHeuristics: greedy, local search
11.3Baselines: exhaustive and random search

W11 · N.4

StrategyWhat it doesComplexityOptimal?
Exhaustive searchEvaluates all (n−1)!/2 toursO(n!)Yes
Random searchEvaluates k random tours, keeps the bestO(kn): k tours, O(n) to score eachBy chance; closer as k grows
11.4Greedy construction: nearest neighbour

W11 · N.5

A greedy algorithm constructs a solution step by step, optimising only the local decision at each step. Nearest neighbour starts at a city and always travels to the nearest unvisited city, then returns to the start.

It takes n − 1 steps, each scanning up to n cities: O(n²). It never looks ahead to the closing edge, so the forced last leg can be long.

State how you broke ties, and do not forget the return leg when totalling a tour.

11.5Greedy construction: cheapest-side insertion

W11 · N.6

  • Start with the closest pair of cities as a two-city tour.
  • Repeatedly take the outside city x closest to a city y on the tour.
  • Insert x next to y on whichever side of y adds less to the tour length. Check both sides.

As written, each step searches all (outside, tour) pairs in O(n²), over n steps: O(n³). The two greedy methods need not agree.

11.6Local search and 2-opt

W11 · N.7

Greedy constructs a solution, so there is no complete answer until it finishes. Local search starts from a complete solution and repeatedly makes a small modification that improves it. It stops at a local optimum, where no small modification helps, or when time runs out.

AdvantageDisadvantage
More iterations tend to approach the optimumA very bad start may need many iterations
You can stop at any time and still hold a complete solutionIt can get stuck at a local optimum that is not the global one

2-opt deletes 2 edges of the tour and reconnects the pieces into a different valid tour, which amounts to reversing a segment. The first edge has n choices, the second must not share a city with it (n − 3 choices), and each pair is counted twice, so the neighbourhood has n(n−3)/2 = O(n²) tours: 9 for n = 6.

11.7Greedy beyond TSP, and when it fails

W11 · N.8

Greedy is a general design idea. Taking the locally best choice can leave an awkward remainder that a better early choice would have avoided.

ProblemGreedy ruleFailure
Coin change with 100, 60, 35, 5, 1Take the largest coin that fits70¢: greedy gives 60 + 5 + 5 (3 coins); 35 + 35 uses 2
0/1 knapsack, 7 kg limitAdd the item with the best value per kilogramTakes E then D ($11) and B no longer fits; B + E gives $14
Maximum-sum root-to-leaf pathMove to the larger childGreedy 8 → 21 → 9 → 12 gives 50; 8 → 2 → 67 → 14 gives 91
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The five strategies for TSP, named as the course names them.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Exhaustive searchEvaluates every tour.Optimal but O(n!).
Random searchScores k random tours.O(kn), optimal only by chance.
Nearest neighbourGreedy: always go to the nearest unvisited city (also called greedy algorithm 1).O(n²); ignores the closing edge.
Cheapest-side insertionGreedy: insert the outside city next to its nearest tour city, on the cheaper side (also called greedy algorithm 2).O(n³) as written.
2-optLocal search: delete 2 edges and reconnect.Starts from a complete tour.

Genetic algorithms, which keep a population of tours, are a further heuristic idea in the notes; they are not one of these five strategies.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 11.1

Nearest neighbour in Ireland

The problem

Start at Belfast with Cork, Dublin, Galway and Limerick. Ties are broken towards Cork.

The trace
StepFromChoose (distance)Tour length so far
1BelfastDublin (167)334, closed
2DublinLimerick (198)688, closed

4CorkGalway (209), the last one985, closed

The optimal tour Belfast, Galway, Limerick, Cork, Dublin is 940 km, so nearest neighbour is about 5% worse.

The lesson

The forced final leg Galway to Belfast costs 306 km: nearest neighbour never looks ahead.

WORKED EXAMPLE 11.2

Greedy coin change fails

The problem

Coins 100, 60, 35, 5, 1. Pay 70.

The trace
  • Greedy takes 60, leaving 10, then 5 and 5: three coins.
  • The optimum is 35 + 35: two coins.
The lesson

A large early coin can leave a remainder that needs many small coins.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
How big is brute force?. For the six-place Singapore day trip, how many distinct tours must exhaustive search consider? How many if costs depend on direction? Report counts and times for n = 10, 15, 20 at 10⁹ tours per second.
Show answer
Symmetric, six places: (6−1)!/2 = 60. Direction-dependent: (6−1)! = 120. At 10⁹ tours/s: n = 10 has 181,440 tours (about 0.0002 s); n = 15 has 43,589,145,600 (about 44 s); n = 20 has about 6.1 × 10¹⁶ (about 1.9 years). Going from n to n + 1 multiplies the count by n.
2
Nearest neighbour from J and from S. Distances (km): C–J 28, C–N 25, C–P 13, C–S 17, C–W 24, J–N 6, J–P 19, J–S 11, J–W 13, N–P 17, N–S 10, N–W 16, P–S 12, P–W 12, S–W 17. Run nearest neighbour from J and from S.
Show answer
From J: J → N (6) → S (10) → P (12) → W (12) → C (24) → J (28), total 92 km. From S: S → N (10) → J (6) → W (13) → P (12) → C (13) → S (17), total 71 km. The start matters: nearest neighbour is not optimal and the closing leg is never considered. The optimal tour for this data is also 71 km.
3
Cheapest-side insertion. Build a tour of the same six places by cheapest-side insertion and compare with nearest neighbour.
Show answer
Start with the closest pair, J and N (6 km). Repeatedly take the outside place closest to a place on the tour and insert it on whichever side of that place adds less. Check both sides, and state how you broke ties because several insertions cost the same. Then compare the final length with 92 km (from J) and 71 km (from S).
4
Improve a tour with 2-opt. Starting from the tour J, N, S, P, W, C (92 km), apply 2-opt with best improvement until no move helps. How many 2-opt neighbours does a six-place tour have?
Show answer
A six-place tour has 6(6−3)/2 = 9 neighbours. Best-improvement steps: 92 km, then J, N, S, P, C, W at 78 km, then J, N, S, C, P, W at 71 km, after which no 2-opt move improves. A local optimum need not be a global optimum in general; here 71 km happens to match the best tour.
5
When greedy coin change fails. Coins 1, 5, 6, 9, unlimited. For amounts 11, 12 and 15 give the greedy and an optimal combination.
Show answer
11: greedy 9 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), optimal 5 + 6 (2). 12: greedy 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 (4), optimal 6 + 6 (2). 15: greedy 9 + 6 (2), which is optimal. So largest-coin-first fails for this coin system.
6
Compare the strategies. Compare exhaustive TSP, random TSP search (k tours), nearest neighbour, 2-opt local search and greedy coin change for coins 1, 5, 10, 50.
Show answer
Exhaustive: O(n!) work, works for any input, guaranteed optimal. Random search: O(kn), any input, no guarantee. Nearest neighbour: O(n²), any input, no guarantee. 2-opt: O(n²) per iteration, any starting tour, ends at a local optimum with no guarantee of the global optimum. Greedy coin change for 1, 5, 10, 50: very cheap, and optimal for that particular coin system.
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Counting TSP routes for 20 cities. How many routes need to be examined for 20 cities with symmetric distances, and with direction-dependent distances?
Show answer
Symmetric: 19!/2. Direction-dependent: 19!.
2
Two greedy tours on seven cities. From the distance table on the sheet, give the tour from the first greedy algorithm starting at A, and from the second greedy algorithm starting with the closest pair.
Show answer
Answer key: nearest neighbour A → D → C → G → E → F → B → A with cost 861 (its mirror is also fine). Cheapest-side insertion C → D → A → G → E → F → B → C with cost 816 (mirrors and rotations are also fine).
3
Greedy path in a tree. The greedy rule moves to the child with the higher value from the root to a leaf. Apply it to the tutorial tree, then give a tree where it fails.
Show answer
On the tutorial tree greedy gives 8 + 21 + 9 + 12 = 50. A failure example from the key: greedy takes the path with sum 1 + 3 = 4 while the optimal path is 1 + 2 + 5 = 8, because a smaller child can lead to a much larger descendant.
4
Coins 20, 10, 5, 1. Design a brute-force and a greedy algorithm for change. Does greedy ever fail for these coins?
Show answer
Brute force: try all subsets of size 1, then size 2, and so on, until one pays the amount. Greedy: repeatedly deduct the largest denomination that fits. For 20, 10, 5, 1 greedy never fails (answer: no).
5
Knapsack with a 15 kg bag. Items A (12 kg, $10), B (5 kg, $8), C (4 kg, $2), D (3 kg, $5), E (2 kg, $6). Describe brute force and greedy, and say whether greedy can fail for some limit.
Show answer
Brute force: try all subsets (5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 combinations by size). Greedy: repeatedly add the item with the best value-to-weight ratio until the limit would be breached; a smallest-weight-first rule is another option. Greedy can fail, for example with a 7 kg limit (E then D gives $11, but B + E gives $14).
⚡ Quick examples
Counting tours
PointDivide by n for the start and by 2 for direction.
Example5 cities give 4!/2 = 12 tours.
ExplanationA tour is a cycle and its reverse has equal length.
Stopping local search
PointStop at a local optimum or when time ends.
ExampleNo 2-opt move shortens the tour.
ExplanationA local optimum may not be the global optimum.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • TSP has (n−1)!/2 tours for symmetric distances; (n−1)! if asymmetric.
  • Pick two of general, optimal and fast; heuristics are fast and general.
  • Exhaustive search is optimal in O(n!); random search is O(kn).
  • Nearest neighbour is O(n²); cheapest-side insertion is O(n³); neither is optimal.
  • Local search improves a complete solution until a local optimum; 2-opt has n(n−3)/2 neighbours.
  • Greedy can fail on coin change, knapsack and tree paths.

lessons.title: Limits of Computation
lessons.goal: Separate solving from verifying, and place problems in P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Some problems may have no efficient exact algorithm. Knowing which ones tells you when to use heuristics.
🧠 Memory hook
Solve is hard, verify is easy. NP is about verifying a proposed answer in polynomial time.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
How bad is bad growth?Efficient algorithms and tractable problemsSolving against verifyingThe classes P and NPReductions and NP-complete problemsNP-hard problemsP = NP?
⚡ At a glance — the class relationships
P ⊆ NPNP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NPP = NP is unproven
12.1How bad is bad growth?

W13 · O.1

Times at one operation per nanosecond:

nO(n)O(n²)O(2ⁿ)O(n!)
100.01 μs0.1 μs1 μs3.63 ms
200.02 μs0.4 μs1 ms77.1 years
300.03 μs0.9 μs1 s8 × 10¹⁵ years
1000.1 μs10 μs4 × 10¹³ years–
12.2Efficient algorithms and tractable problems

W13 · O.2

TermDefinition
Efficient algorithmPolynomial time or lower: O(nᵏ) for some constant k
Inefficient algorithmExponential O(kⁿ) or factorial O(n!)
Tractable problemA known solution with polynomial complexity or lower exists
Intractable problemNo known polynomial-time solution
12.3Solving against verifying

W13 · O.3

Multiplying 3 × 5 is instant, but finding the factors of 15 needs a search. At scale, factoring a 212-digit number took about 2,000 CPU-years, yet given the two factors, checking them is a single multiplication.

Subset sum taskMethodCost
Solve by brute forceTry all 2ⁿ subsets and sum each in O(n)O(2ⁿ × n)
Verify a proposed subsetAdd its elements and compare with 0O(n)

Does any subset of [11, 5, −3, −1, −2, 7, −4] sum to 0? Yes: {5, −1, −4}.

12.4The classes P and NP

W13 · O.4

ClassDefinitionExamples
P (Polynomial)A known polynomial-time algorithm solves itMultiplication, sorting, closest pair O(n log n), shortest path O(n²)
NP (Non-deterministic Polynomial)A proposed solution can be verified in polynomial timePrime factorisation, subset sum, and everything in P

P ⊆ NP: if you can solve a problem in polynomial time, you can verify an answer by solving and comparing. NP does not stand for "not polynomial".

12.5Reductions and NP-complete problems

W13 · O.5

A reduction shows that problem 1 is a special case of problem 2, by converting any instance of problem 1 into an instance of problem 2. An algorithm for problem 2 then also solves problem 1, so problem 1 is no harder than problem 2.

  • Subtraction to addition: compute A − B as A + (−B).
  • Integer sorting to topological sort: make one vertex per integer and an edge u → v whenever u < v; a topological order of this DAG is the sorted order.
  • Hamiltonian cycle to TSP.

NP-complete examples: subset sum and Boolean satisfiability (SAT).

12.6NP-hard problems

W13 · O.6

NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. A problem can be NP-hard without being in NP.

  • TSP, optimisation version: find the minimum-length tour. Given a tour you can check that it is a tour, but not easily that it is the shortest. So it is NP-hard rather than NP-complete.
  • Graph colouring: colour the vertices with the minimum number of colours so that adjacent vertices differ.
12.7P = NP?

W13 · O.7

If P = NPIf P ≠ NP
Hard problems become solvable: hope for optimal TSP in polynomial timeWe keep relying on approximations and heuristics for these problems
Much cryptography, such as RSA, would collapse, since it relies on problems that are hard to solve but easy to checkCryptographic assumptions stay plausible

Most computer scientists believe P ≠ NP, but it has not been proven.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The four problem classes of this chapter.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
PSolvable in polynomial time by a known algorithm.Solving is easy.
NPA proposed answer can be verified in polynomial time.Verifying is easy; contains P.
NP-completeIn NP, and as hard as any problem in NP.NP-hard ∩ NP.
NP-hardAt least as hard as the NP-complete problems; need not be in NP.Optimisation TSP: the answer cannot be checked easily.

NP does not stand for "not polynomial", and NP-hard does not mean "in NP".

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 12.1

Subset sum: solve against verify

The problem

Decide whether some subset of [11, 5, −3, −1, −2, 7, −4] sums to 0.

The trace
  • Solving by brute force tries all 2⁷ = 128 subsets.
  • Verifying the proposed subset {5, −1, −4}: 5 − 1 − 4 = 0, one pass.
The lesson

Checking a given answer is cheap; finding one is the hard part.

⚡ Quick examples
Reduction
PointConvert one problem into another and reuse the solver.
ExampleSubtraction A − B as addition A + (−B).
ExplanationProblem 1 is no harder than problem 2.
NP-complete
PointThe intersection of NP-hard and NP.
ExampleSubset sum and SAT.
ExplanationIn NP, and as hard as any problem in NP.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Exponential and factorial growth become infeasible even for small n.
  • Efficient means polynomial; tractable means a known polynomial solution exists.
  • P: solvable in polynomial time. NP: verifiable in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP.
  • A reduction converts problem 1 into problem 2, so problem 1 is no harder.
  • NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP; optimisation TSP is NP-hard.
  • P = NP is unproven; if P ≠ NP, heuristics remain necessary.

mcq.q: A standard deck has 4 suits. What is the minimum number of cards you must draw to guarantee at least 3 cards of the same suit?
mcq.e: Pigeonhole: k(m−1)+1 = 4×2+1 = 9. With 8 cards you could hold exactly 2 of each suit.

mcq.q: 100 people are in a room. What is the largest number *n* such that at least *n* of them are guaranteed to share a birth month?
mcq.e: 12 months × 8 = 96 < 100, so some month has at least 9 people. (97 people are already enough.)

mcq.q: A licence plate has 3 letters (A–Z) followed by 4 digits (0–9). Letters and digits may repeat. How many plates are possible?
mcq.e: Seven independent positions, so the product rule gives 26³ × 10⁴ = 175,760,000.

mcq.q: Same plate format as Q3, but no letter may repeat and no digit may repeat. How many plates are possible?
mcq.e: Order matters (plates), so use permutations: P(26,3) × P(10,4) = 15,600 × 5,040 = 78,624,000. B is the combination mistake C(26,3)×C(10,4).

mcq.q: A set meal is either a starter + main or a main + dessert. There are 5 starters, 8 mains and 4 desserts. How many different set meals?
mcq.e: Product rule inside each option: 5×8 = 40 and 8×4 = 32. The two options cannot overlap (one has a starter, the other a dessert), so the sum rule gives 72.

mcq.q: In a class of 40, 25 take Python, 18 take Java and 8 take both. How many take neither?
mcq.e: Inclusion–exclusion: |P ∪ J| = 25 + 18 − 8 = 35. Neither = 40 − 35 = 5.

mcq.q: A PIN has 4 digits (0–9, leading zeros allowed). How many PINs contain at least one repeated digit?
mcq.e: Complement rule: total 10⁴ = 10,000 minus all-distinct 10×9×8×7 = 5,040 → 4,960.

mcq.q: How many 3-letter strings (letters A–Z, repeats allowed) contain at least one vowel (A, E, I, O, U)?
mcq.e: Complement: 26³ − 21³ = 17,576 − 9,261 = 8,315 (21 consonants).

mcq.q: Ten runners finish a race. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded?
mcq.e: Swap test: gold and silver are different outcomes → permutation. P(10,3) = 10×9×8 = 720.

mcq.q: A committee of 4 (no special roles) is chosen from 12 people. How many committees?
mcq.e: Order does not matter: C(12,4) = 495. C is P(12,4), which overcounts by 4! = 24.

mcq.q: A group has 5 men and 6 women. How many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?
mcq.e: C(6,2) × C(5,2) = 15 × 10 = 150 (product rule on two independent choices).

mcq.q: Same group (5 men, 6 women). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?
mcq.e: Complement: all committees C(11,4) = 330 minus all-men committees C(5,4) = 5 → 325.

mcq.q: 7 different books are placed on a shelf. Three of them (a trilogy) must be next to each other, in any order. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Block method: block + 4 others = 5 objects → 5! = 120, times 3! = 6 internal orders = 720. (1,440 would be 6!×2.)

mcq.q: Same 7 books, but the trilogy must be together in the order Vol 1, Vol 2, Vol 3. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: The block has only one internal order, so just 5! = 120.

mcq.q: 5 boys and 3 girls stand in a row (all different people). No two girls may stand next to each other. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Gap method: arrange the boys 5! = 120, creating 6 gaps. Choose 3 gaps C(6,3) = 20 and arrange the girls 3! = 6. 120×20×6 = 14,400. (C = forgetting to arrange the girls.)

mcq.q: 7 different people sit around a round table. Rotations count as the same arrangement. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Fix one person, arrange the other 6: (7−1)! = 720.

mcq.q: 7 different people sit around a round table (rotations are the same). Two particular people, Amy and Ben, must sit next to each other. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Treat Amy+Ben as one block → 6 objects in a circle → (6−1)! = 120, times 2! for the block's internal order = 240. (B forgets the circular reduction.)

mcq.q: A bracelet is made from 6 different beads. Two bracelets are the same if one can be rotated or flipped over to match the other. How many different bracelets?
mcq.e: Circular arrangements (6−1)! = 120; reflections are identified in pairs, so divide by 2: 60.

mcq.q: How many 4-digit numbers (1000 to 9999) are there if digits may repeat?
mcq.e: First digit 9 choices (not 0), each of the other three 10 choices: 9×10³. C (9×9×8×7) is the all-distinct count.

mcq.q: How many 3-digit numbers (100 to 999) have all different digits and are even?
mcq.e:
Split by the last digit:
• Last digit 0: first digit 9 choices, middle 8 → 72.
• Last digit 2, 4, 6 or 8 (4 choices): first digit can't be 0 or the last digit → 8 choices; middle digit can't be either used digit → 8 choices → 4×8×8 = 256.
Total 72 + 256 = 328 (sum rule over disjoint cases). C (648) is all 3-digit numbers with distinct digits, ignoring "even".

mcq.q: 12 people at a party each shake hands exactly once with every other person. How many handshakes?
mcq.e: A handshake is an unordered pair: C(12,2) = 66.

mcq.q: How many 8-bit binary strings start with 1 or end with 00?
mcq.e: Inclusion–exclusion: start with 1 = 2⁷ = 128; end with 00 = 2⁶ = 64; both = 2⁵ = 32. 128 + 64 − 32 = 160.

mcq.q: How many 8-bit binary strings contain exactly three 1s?
mcq.e: Choose which 3 of the 8 positions hold a 1: C(8,3) = 56. (C is P(8,3).)

def m(a):

    mid = len(a) // 2

    right = m(a[mid:])

mcq.e: The replacement is either the right-most node of the left subtree (3 → 6 → 7, so 7) or the left-most node of the right subtree (10 has no left child, so 10).

mcq.e: Sorted insertion makes every node the right child of the previous one (a linked list), so searching for 50 compares all 5 nodes. Inserting 30 first, then the middles of each half, would give a balanced tree instead.

mcq.q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree with 5 levels (root is level 1)?
mcq.e: Each level can double: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 2⁵ − 1 = 31.

mcq.e: Height ≈ ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10, and the worst-case comparisons equal the tree's height.

mcq.e: Swaps = number of inversions: 5 is before 2, 4, 1, 3 (4); 2 before 1 (1); 4 before 1, 3 (2); 6 before 1, 3 (2). Total 9.

mcq.e: Each of the 9 later elements is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put (best case O(n)).

mcq.e: Pass 1: smallest is 11, swap with 64 → [11, 25, 12, 22, 64]. Pass 2: smallest of the rest is 12, swap with 25 → [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]. (B is after one pass.)

mcq.e: Big-O describes growth for large n, not exact running time. For small n, or with large constants, an O(2ⁿ) algorithm can be quicker, so "always" makes the statement false. The other statements are true.

def f(a, upper=None):

    if upper <= 1: return 1
    else: return f(a, floor(sqrt(upper)))
mcq.e: The argument goes n → n^(1/2) → n^(1/4) → …, so after k calls it is n^(1/2ᵏ). It reaches about 2 when 2ᵏ ≈ log₂ n, so k ≈ log₂(log₂ n).

        return 0
    else:
        return h(n-1) + h(n-1)
mcq.e: If n is odd, n−1 is even, so both recursive calls return 0 immediately. There are at most 3 calls in total, so the cost is constant.

def x(n):
    sum = 0
    for i in range(n):
        j = 1
        while (j < 2**i):
            j = j * 2
            sum = sum * j
    return sum
mcq.e: For a given i, j doubles from 1 up to 2ⁱ, so the while loop runs log₂(2ⁱ) = i times. The total is 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2, which is O(n²).

mcq.q: Mock exam Q15. What is the best-case time complexity of selection sort?
mcq.e: Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted part, so it makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons in every case. Insertion sort is the one with an O(n) best case.

mcq.q: Mock exam Q16. What is the worst-case time complexity of selection sort?
mcq.e: The comparison count is n(n−1)/2 for every input, so the worst case is also O(n²).

mcq.q: Mock exam Q17. How many swaps does selection sort make in its best case, an already sorted list?
mcq.e: It swaps only when the current position does not already hold the smallest remaining item. A sorted list needs no swaps, although it still makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons. The worst case is at most n − 1 swaps.

mcq.q: Mock exam Q18. Merge sort (mid = len(a)//2) sorts X = [50, 16, 23, 44, 16, 9, 5, 20, 72, 56, 16]. What does the 6th call of merge2 return?
mcq.e: The left half is finished first (5 merges, ending with [16,16,23,44,50]). In the right half [9,5,20,72,56,16], mid = 3 gives [9,5,20]. That splits into [9] and [5,20]: merge 5 gives [5,20] and merge 6 combines [9] with it to give [5,9,20].

mcq.q: Mock exam Q21. What is the time complexity of the brute-force closest-pair algorithm, which examines every pair of integers?
mcq.e: There are n(n−1)/2 pairs and each takes constant time, so the total is O(n²).

wr.q: Mock exam Q6. Write the recursive equivalent of the iterative `isSorted(a)`.
wr.a:
Index version, O(n):

def isSorted(a, i=0):
    if i >= len(a) - 1:       # 0 or 1 elements left: sorted
        return True
    if a[i] > a[i+1]:         # out-of-order pair
        return False
    return isSorted(a, i + 1) # check the rest

The slicing version return a[0] < a[1] and isSorted(a[1:]) is also acceptable but copies lists, so it costs O(n²).

Marking points: correct base case, comparison of adjacent elements, returning False on a violation, and a recursive call on a smaller problem.

wr.q: Mock exam Q8. Sorting with two stacks. Inside the loop while currentInt < topStack, the top of stack is moved to tempstack. Fill in the two blanks: (1) how to look at the new top of stack without removing it, and (2) how to move the larger elements back.
wr.a:
Answer 1: stack[-1], a peek. stack.pop() would delete the element.

Answer 2: stack.append(tempstack.pop()). The larger elements went to tempstack largest-first, so the smallest of them is on top and must sit just above currentInt. Popping them one by one restores ascending order.

Trace on [3,1,2] gives [1,2,3]. Worst case is O(n²).

wr.q:
Mock exam Q19. Complete the recursive merge. The blanks are answer 1, answer 2 and answer 3.
def merge3(a1, a2, i=0, j=0):
    if i < len(a1) or j < len(a2):
        if (j == len(a2)) or (i < len(a1) and a1[i] < a2[j]):
            return [ a1[i] ] + merge3(__answer1__)
        else:
            return [ a2[j] ] + merge3(__answer2__)
    return __answer3__
wr.a:
Answer 1: a1, a2, i+1, j
Answer 2: a1, a2, i, j+1
Answer 3: []

i and j replace the loop variables of the iterative merge. Taking a1[i] advances i, and taking a2[j] advances j. When both lists are exhausted the base case returns the empty list, the identity for +. Common mistakes: forgetting to pass a1, a2, returning None, and writing i++.

wr.q:
Mock exam Q20. Complete the stack-based merge. The stack holds the state (i, j) that the recursive version passes as arguments.
def stk_merge3(a1, a2):
    stk = Stack(); stk.push(0); stk.push(0)
    r = []
    while stk.count() > 0:
        i = stk.pop(); j = stk.pop()
        if i < len(a1) or j < len(a2):
            if (j == len(a2)) or (i < len(a1) and a1[i] < a2[j]):
                r.append(a1[i]); stk.push(j); stk.push(i+1)
            else:
                r.append(__answer1__)
                stk.push(__answer2__)
                stk.push(__answer3__)
    return r
wr.a:
Answer 1: a2[j]
Answer 2: j+1
Answer 3: i

Push order matters: i is popped first and then j, so j is pushed first and i last. In the else branch j advances and i is unchanged. When neither index is in range nothing is pushed, the stack empties and the loop ends.

wr.q: Mock exam Q22. Describe a better algorithm than brute force for the closest pair of integers in a list of `n` integers, with its worst-case complexity.
wr.a:
Sort, then compare adjacent elements: O(n log n).

def closest_pair(a):
    b = sorted(a)                  # merge sort: O(n log n)
    best_pair, best_dist = (b[0], b[1]), b[1] - b[0]
    for k in range(1, len(b) - 1): # one pass: O(n)
        d = b[k+1] - b[k]
        if d < best_dist:
            best_dist, best_pair = d, (b[k], b[k+1])
    return best_pair

After sorting, the closest pair must be adjacent: if x < y < z then |x−z| is at least as large as both |x−y| and |y−z|. The total is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the scan. With insertion or selection sort the total would be O(n²), no better than brute force.
